subtopic: REPEAL OP PROVISION RESPECTING GRATUITY IN LIEU OF LEAVE ON RETIREMENT

speechtext:
Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of National Revenue) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 55, to amend the Department of National Revenue Act.

He said: In all departments of government when employees are superannuated because of age, they are given a certain period of leave of absence. In the Department of National Revenue their pensions start at the beginning of that period but in other departments of government the pension starts at the end of that period. There is a difference in treatment between the employees of the Department of National Revenue and those of other departments, and the purpose of this bill is to provide that the officers of the Department of National Revenue shall receive the same treatment in this respect as the employees of other departments.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: REPEAL OP PROVISION RESPECTING GRATUITY IN LIEU OF LEAVE ON RETIREMENT
speechtext:
It will be remembered
that a custom grew up whereby those who on retirement were given six months' leave with pay might begin at once to receive their pension. The six months' salary was paid when the leave began, less the amount of pension for that period, thus enabling pension to begin immediately on leave being granted.

subtopic: REPEAL OP PROVISION RESPECTING GRATUITY IN LIEU OF LEAVE ON RETIREMENT

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, March 5, consideration of the motion of Hon. Charles A. Dunning (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Bennett.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the house were logical in its deliberations I think the amendment that has been moved by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) should receive unanimous support. I make that dbservation because in previous years members of the Liberal party, when in opposition, supported motions of this kind. L might go back to March of the year 1930 when a similar motion was moved in this chamber, and every Conservative member voted in favour of the Liberal government taking action to deal with the problem of unemployment. Then in 1931, after the Conservative party had been in power for a little over a year, a motion was presented on going into supply asking the government to
15SS
The Budget-Mr. Heaps

take definite and immediate action to cope with the problem of unemployment, and every Liberal member of the house supported it. If therefore on this occasion I asked Liberal members to vote for the amendment I would be asking them to do just what they did in previous years. Even as late as 1935, to which reference has been made already, the Liberal party supported an amendment of this kind.
I think it will be recognized on all sides, and in fact I believe it was admitted by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) in his address on Tuesday last, that up to the present time the government have not been able to take effective action to deal with the unemployment problem in Canada. I think, further, it is generally recognized that there is no question, other than perhaps the question of peace or war, that is of such vital importance to the people of this country as the question of unemployment. It was unemployment and the economic conditions prevailing in the country in 1930 that brought about the change of government that occurred at that time. I also believe it was the unemployment situation and the economic condition of the country in 1935 that brought about the change of government that occurred in that year. Therefore if any government, whether it be Liberal or Conservative, does not deal in am effective way with the unemployment problem its chances of being returned to power at a subsequent election are very slight indeed. So it is evident that if this government hopes to be returned to office at another election it must deal effectively with this pressing problem.
For the moment, Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal with some of the remedies that have been suggested and applied by parliament during the past six or seven years. In 1930, as most hon. members will recall, unemployment was to be cured by increasing tariffs and by preventing the dumping of goods into this country. By the process of an increase in tariff on all goods entering Canada, and anti-dumping duties, we were to solve the problem of unemployment. As the years went by, however, the failure of that theory became more and more apparent, until in 1934 it was more or less abandoned and the government of the day began to introduce social legislation, which has since been declared ultra vires by the highest court of the empire. In other words it may be said that those who at one time believed the problem of unemployment might be solved by increasing the tariffs of Canada realize to-day perhaps more than ever before that the desired result cannot be achieved in that way. The present government believes it can deal with the unemployment situation in the opposite way. The Con-

servative party when in power expected to solve the unemployment problem by increasing tariffs; the party now in power expects to solve the problem by decreasing tariffs. In my humble opinion, Mr. Speaker, just as the increases in our tariffs were ineffective in dealing with the question of unemployment, so any reductions in our tariffs will also be ineffective.
The policy of the present government, according to the statements that have been made, is to solve the unemployment problem by increasing our trade with the other nations of the world. I do not think there is one member of this house, regardless of what political party he may support, who is not in favour of increasing our trade with other countries. I do feel, however, that so far as increased trade with the other nations is concerned, the tariff structure of a country to-day, is not as important as it may have been years ago. There are so many other factors affecting the problem, that while it may be desirable for a number of reasons to have lower tariffs both in Canada and in other countries, we have reached a stage in our economic development where the tariff structure is a less important factor than it has been in previous years.
I should like to call attention to some of the election literature issued by the Liberal party during the last campaign. I do not think it is unfair to say that the policy of the Liberal party, as expressed in some of the publications issued from the headquarters in Ottawa, was to the effect that by making treaties with other nations of the world and by reducing our own tariffs we should extend our trade so that other nations might obtain the goods we produce. If this policy fails, as I believe ultimately it must, then I wonder what the policy of the government is going to be. So far they have not indicated what their policy is to be with respect to the unemployment situation. It is admitted by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) that there are
400,000	men and women out of employment. There are over 1,000,000 persons in receipt of public relief, and yet not one definite word have we had from the government as to what its real policy will be.
I know they will come to us and say, "We have appointed a commission to deal with the unemployment problem." But despite the fact that the government has been in power since October, 1935, and despite the appointment of a commission, the results up to this time have not been satisfactory. The commission has done nothing which could not have been done had it not been in existence. A home improvement plan was recommended in 1935; there is nothing new in the farm

The Budget-Mr. Heaps
placement scheme, to deal with the single men. When the Minister of Labour spoke on Tuesday last he dwelt at length with what the government had done to deal with the single unemployed. After the speech of the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) I believe no hon. member will again refer to what the government has done in coping with the problem of unemployed single men.
People in Canada expect something more than a policy of inaction such as the government has followed. It would seem that, Micawber-like, the government is hoping that ultimately something may turn up. But nothing is likely to turn up unless the party in power is prepared to take definite and effective action. On many occasions hon. members have been asked what concrete suggestions they have to offer. My suggestion would be that the government look to the sister dominions. Look at what New Zealand has done since the new government took office a little more than a year ago. May I read from a communication sent to a party in Winnipeg, and later published in a Winnipeg paper, in regard to some of the experiments which were tried in New Zealand and proved to be effective. I wonder if our government will be good enough to follow the example set by this sister dominion. This is what, in part, was written:
Our labour government is in recess, after a most strenuous session in which it has put more bills through than any other government before, viz: taken over the transport of the country; passed the forty-hour-week bill, with forty-four hours for shops; taken over the Reserve bank which controls the finances of the country; taken over the control of butter and cheese (the farmer now gets a fixed price for same and is better off); . . .
May I here interpose that no farmer in Canada would object to the same thing being done right here.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
"Oh, my child, you cannot eat from that cupboard; we must wait until people somewhere else are satisfied. When they have all they want I might let you have a few crumbs from our own cupboard." Obviously that state of affairs in any household would be ridiculous. Immediately the child would say to its mother, "Why can I not have some of the things in the cupboard? They belong to us; we have produced them; why can we not eat them?" But the mother would say, "No, my child, wait until the people a few streets away are satisfied, and then you may have anything that is left in the cupboard." The same reasoning would apply to the situation in Canada. Our people .beg of us, "We want the goods we have produced; we want foodstuffs, clothing and shelter." But we say to them, "No, you cannot have those goods 'until we have satisfied the demand in China"-or in Japan, Germany, France or some other part of the world. If for a number of reasons the people in those other parts of the world are not able to obtain or to purchase the goods we have to! offer, then our own people must go without them. Is there any hon. member who will say that that is the logical thing to do? Certainly not. That is why I say, when we speak about satisfying foreign markets and creating a foreign demand, that the first thing we ought to do is to satisfy the demand for goods in the Dominion of Canada.
I pointed out that in New Zealand they have attempted to do something to cope with this problem, and I sincerely hope that some of the things which have been adopted there will be adopted here. The government cannot shield itself indefinitely behind the British North America Act. If there is a will to d!o something for the people of Canada, I think the way can be found to overcome this obstacle which is inherent in our constitution. If, as has' been stated, it is the declared policy of the government to wait until the provinces do something, then I am afraid this parliament is in a state of absolute despair. If we have to wait until all the nine provinces of Canada agree upon a definite and fixed policy, we may have to wait many a long day before this parliament will be able to do something in a concrete way to deal with the pressing problems which now confront us.
It has been stated by the Liberal party that the policy of expanding markets has been one of the means of easing this problem. That party also takes credit for the fact that during the past twelve or eighteen months there has been a decided increase in our export trade,

which they claim is diue to the treaties made with other countries. I cannot subscribe to that theory. Rightly or wrongly, I am of the opinion that if we had made but little change in our tariff structure-in passing I may say that I am always in favour of lower tariffs-there would still have been an increase in the trade of this country with other nations of the world. The worst year that we had from the standpoint of imports and exports was 1932, but from that time onward there has been a steady improvement in the amount of goods exported from this country, and also an improvement in the amount of goods imported. I am always loth to quote figures, but on this occasion perhaps it would not be out of place. I should like to give some figures recently published by the bureau of statistics.
The first figures I shall give refer to trade with the United Kingdom. I find that in 1932 our exports to Great Britain amounted to $178,171,000 in round figures. In 1935 they had increased to $306,897,000, and for the calendar year 1936 they had jumped to $399,-
830,000.	I do not think anyone can claim that the tariff structure as between the two countries was the dominating factor in that tremendous increase in trade. As was pointed out the other day by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol), much of this increase was the result of the tremendous demand in Great Britain for supplies and materials for armament purposes.
We find practically the same increase in trade with other countries where there have been no new trade agreements entered into during the past five years. Both New Zealand and Australia show practically the same results. When the government took credit for the boosting of trade between the United States and this country through the medium of the trade treaty, I do not think their argument was sound. The United States have spent tens of billions of dollars in an effort to improve economic conditions, and part of that increased business was bound to come to this dominion. When we consider the amount of money spent by the United States on their home improvement plan it is quite easy to understand why there has been such a huge increase in the trade between the province of British Columbia and that country. The trade treaty signed a year ago was only a negligible factor in the increase of trade between Canada and the United States.
I have pointed out, and I still maintain, that increases in the tariff will not solve our problem. Neither will decreases. If this government, or any party which may be in power,

The Budget-Mr. Heaps
expects to improve the economic condition of this country or grapple seriously with the problem of unemployment, it will have to go far deeper into our economic structure than merely tinkering with the tariff. Our whole system of production to-day is based on the profit motive. The minute a firm is not making a profit, production begins to slow down or ceases entirely. We in our group contend that the profit motive must give way to a higher one. The production of commodities must ibe carried on for the purpose of satisfying the legitimate demands of the people of this dominion.
The factors of production and consumption must be closely correlated. If we increase our production, as we have in years gone by, by leaps and bounds, and our consumption does not keep pace, then just as surely as night follows day we are bound to create an unemployment problem or aggravate one which may already exist. The spread between production and consumption is an indication and guide to our unemployment situation. The larger the spread there is between wages and production or consumption, the greater will be our unemployment problem. Unless our purchasing power or consumptive opportunities are correlated in some way to the question of production, then our unemployment problem will continue and remain with us for many a long day to come. It is only by increasing our consumptive opportunities, by increasing wages, if you wish to put it that way, and by decreasing the spread between wages and production, that we can tackle this unemployment problem in a definite way.
It has been stated on more than one occasion in this house by the Minister of Labour that the government has in mind a long-term policy of dealing with this problem of unemployment. How long shall we have to wait before being shown that policy? Are we to be shown it just on the eve of an election? We must bear in mind that when this session has been completed, and it is expected it will be over before very long, practically half the life of this parliament will have elapsed, that is if we are to have an election at the end of four years. I believe before the end of the second session of this parliament the people should be told what the definite policy of this government is to cope with the unemployment problem. So far they have not done anything really different from what was done by the government in office between 1930 and 1935, but they have dressed it up in a different way. Instead of relief being handled by the government it is now being handled by a commission, which, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) points out, does not even report to this house. That body was going to coordinate things, to make matters easier as between the dominion government and the governments of the provinces. I do not think anybody in this country takes the commission very seriously. It may act in some measure as a buffer between the federal government and the provinces and municipalities, or it may be a convenient way of "passing the buck," but so far it has not proved effective to cope with the problem of unemployment.
I once described commissions as a convenient way of shelving inconvenient problems; I believe the Prime Minister used similar language a few weeks ago with reference to committees and conferences. The problem of unemployment should be constantly before this chamber; we should not leave it to be dealt with by a body which is not directly responsible to this house.
I am anxious that some time during the debate we shall find out what is the real policy of the government. It was not explained to us the other evening when the Minister of Labour replied to the leader of the opposition. All the minister did was to attempt a defence of the actions of his department in dealing with the single unemployed. Not a ray of hope did he give to our vast army of unemployed scattered all over the dominion. At the present time, when almost half the term of this parliament has expired, all that we can show to the people is a commission, a home improvement plan which they suggested and which is nothing new, a farm placement scheme, and a sort of bureau of statistics which they established on their own account. In my opinion we have in this country a most efficient bureau of statistics and it was unnecessary for the commission to create any new bureau for its own purposes. That seems to be the sum total of the commission's accomplishments since the time it was appointed. It may truly be said that the commission has laboured but has not produced even a mouse.
The Minister of Labour showed great anxiety to bring forward election promises which were made by other political parties. As a rule I do not care to raise these matters, because they speak for themselves. But I recall that huge placards were posted all over my constituency-and other bon. members no doubt had the same experience-stating in big letters, "Vote for King and action." Besides these placards there were hundreds of little stickers, at the top of which appeared the anneal, "Vote Liberal and get action."
The Budget-Mr. Heaps

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am waiting
and the unemployed of this country are waiting for action. What we have had up to now is a period of inaction. It is time that inaction ceased and that we got down to real and definite action to deal with unemployment. I noticed these words in small type in the middle of this little sticker, "Please remove nine days before election day." Evidently it would not do to keep it there too long.
There was a by-election in Toronto in 1933. I remember that when I went down to speak in the constituency this paper I hold in my hand was given to me. Look at the large headlines; they can be seen, I believe, across the aisle. They say, "King banishes fear for workers;" and a huge headline:
Social insurance in Canada to end fear for working class is presaged by the Liberal party leader.
These appeared in a paper published on September 22, 1934. I am still waiting, Mr Speaker, for action, action that will banish fear from the minds of hundreds of thousands who are out of work in the dominion.
What were the specific promises made by the Liberal party? There were many. The first one that comes to my attention is that when they would get into power they would reduce or abolish the sales tax. That was reduced or abolished, was it not? Their method of reducing the tax was to increase it from six per cent to eight per cent, an addition of about thirty-three per cent. Then there was a definite promise that the government would bring in an unemployment insurance bill. Let us see what was said. This is the Prime Minister speaking, I think, over the radio, and reported in a publication of Saturday, August 3. He said:
Unemployment of first concern.
The Liberal party believes unemployment is Canada's most urgent national problem. It would deal with the present emergency conditions, through a representative national commission.
And then he goes on to say:
As permanent measures-
And I want the "hear, bear" of the hon. member to come again after this:
-the Liberal party is pledged to introduce policies which will serve to provide employment by reviving industry and trade; and to introduce a national system of unemployment insurance.
One does not hear any " hear, hear " now from the Liberal side. Instead of that promise being carried out, what have we got? The first thing the Liberal party did when they

got into power was themselves to refer this matter to the privy council, and they got the decision they expected and probably the decision they wanted. In my judgment, Mr. Speaker, there is a tremendous responsibility upon the Liberal party. When pledges are made to the electors they should not be regarded in the lighthearted manner in which they are evidently regarded by some hon. members.

speechtext: We are just as serious as you are.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Now, Mr. Speaker, let us glance at another little publication, one of those handbills which the Liberals distributed by hundreds of thousands:
Tory policies create unemployment. Vote Liberal.
What was the inference? That if one voted for the Liberals their policies would end unemployment in the dominion. Is it in accordance with principles of honest politics that although nearly half the term of this parliament has gone by, and although certain definite policies were promised to the electors, not even an attempt is being made to carry out those promises? I do not think anyone can contend that such political practices are right. One Liberal, however, was not without vision; he evidently had some idea of what was coming-I refer to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie), who, when he was in opposition, made the following cryptic statement:
The majority of the Liberals in the next house is going to be so large that it will be difficult to keep them to their promises. But I promise you that the British Columbia Liberal contingent will live up to its promises.
I should like to see the British Columbia contingent live up to its promises and convince the rest of the Liberal party to go and do likewise. Throughout the country in the last election one of the mottoes of the Liberal party was "work and wages." I am waiting to see the unemployed get the work, and the wages as well, but so far the Liberal party has not provided it. It may not be pleasant for me to bring home to hon. gentlemen opposite some of the promises on which they were elected at the last election. I have before me a little leaflet advising the electorate to " Vote Liberal for work with wages, security and progress." But the people have not the work, nor have they adequate wages, security, and progress. The unemployed cannot be expected to be satisfied with beautiful phrases, which are meaningless when analyzed, as a program of the government. They want something definite, something that will give them

The Budget-Mr. Bothwell
a ray of hope. A commission is not in itself sufficient. To-day the policy of the government is simply to hand out a dole to hundreds of thousands of people out of work, and it is not even creating useful public works. As I have contended before in this house, the provision of public works is in itself no solution of the unemployment problem; it is a palliative which ultimately does not palliate. It merely adds to the national debt and makes it more difficult as time goes on to find further capital expenditures for public relief works.
The Minister of Labour was a professor, and he is a close student of economics. He knows far better than I do that no amount of public works which merely adds to the debt burden of the country can in itself be a solution of the unemployment problem; and when we have to-day, as the only means of coping with unemployment, the home improvement plan, it is only another form of capital expenditure in the attempt to solve the unemployment problem. This capital expenditure is not made, however, by the federal government; it is made by the individual, who is creating a debt for himself which it will take one, two or three years to wipe out. In other words, the poorer classes in Canada are being asked to mortgage their own future earnings in order that they may be able to provide work for themselves and others for the purpose of meeting the unemployment situation. My hope is that the government will take hold of the unemployment problem in a real, effective and fundamental way and see whether they cannot do something to inspire some confidence and hope in the vast number of men and women who are out of work at the present time.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My first word is' one of congratulation to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) on the manner in which the budget address was presented this year. He seems to have covered the situation thoroughly, and he delivered the budget in a manner which I am sure every member of the house will commend.
No matter what policies the government put into effect, every one knows that it will take some little time before the full benefit of those policies can be recognized foy the people. You cannot undo overnight what has been happening over a period of years; you cannot get the full benefit of any policies within a few days after they are put into effect. The immediate question seems to be, what is to be done about unemployment. We all know that it is a serious question, and hon. members, no matter to what party they belong,
are all concerned over the seriousness of it. Everyone in Canada who has anything to do with public affairs is more or less concerned. It will be necessary to have temporary measures of relief for some time to come.
I commend the government for the manner in which they have been administering relief during the sixteen months they have been in office. Late last fall the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) took occasion to visit the constituency I have the honour to represent, and there he had an opportunity to meet the representatives of the councils of eight or nine rural municipalities. He wanted to hear first-hand, suggestions they might have to offer for improvement in the distribution of relief or the better handling of the relief policy, and also any complaints they had to voice. I had an opportunity to sit in at that meeting. These eight or nine municipalities, represented mostly by reeves and secretary treasurers, all had the same word of commendation for the government. They had no difficulties in the municipalities except in one respect; blankets that we supposed to be delivered, as I understood, by the Canadian Red Cross Society, had not yet reached these municipalities. The minister agreed to look into that question, and when a short time later I saw some of these representatives of the municipalities I learned that their troubles on that score had been removed. While the minister was there we should have liked to have had the opportunity of showing him one of the temporary works that might be undertaken to end unemployment in that particular district. For a number of years the people of southwestern Saskatchewan have been agitating for a bridge across the South Saskatchewan river at a place called Saskatchewan Landing. We recognize, of course, that it is a provincial matter, but in the past the federal government has assisted in the construction of bridges across the Saskatchewan river, and we have been hoping that it will at this time continue that work and build a bridge where it is so badly needed.
On February 12 of this year a delegation waited upon the provincial government in Regina. It consisted of the representatives of an association known as the Southwestern Saskatchewan Bridge Association, representatives from the Swift Current board of trade, the council of the city of Swift Current, reeves and councillors of rural municipalities, mayors and councillors of urban municipalities, farm organizations and others. They pressed1 upon the government at Regina the urgent necessity of a bridge at the point in question. At that time they presented all the facts to the provincial government. They were somewhat
The Budget-Mr. Bothwell

encouraged, and were told) that representations would be made to Ottawa. This bridge at Saskatchewan Landing is needed) for various reasons. There is a tremendous amount of traffic there. In fact some 63,320 units cross at Saskatchewan Landing, and they have to cross on a ferry which during the past two or three years has not been working satisfactorily owing to the low water in the river. At certain times of the year the ferry is closed and in order to get to the other side of the river you have to cross in a cage slung from a cable. Vehicles of all descriptions, during the weeks when the ferry is closed, have to drive from one hundred to t.wo hundred miles out of their way to reach the bridge at Elbow.
The areas which would1 be tributary to and served 'by the bridge comprise parts of the richest farming and ranching area of the province, which despite the period of drought has proven its capability to produce enormous agricultural wealth, and is occupied by residents who in normal times produce the best grades of wheat in the world. The area includes approximately eight million acres of rich farm and1 ranch lands. I hardly need call attention to the difficulty of keeping up communication between the south and the north. This bridge is located on No. 4, highway, which extends from the United States border through to Battleford and Prince Albert and the National park, to the northeast. It is a direct connection with a national park south of the United States line, over the Dominion-Ytel'lowstone highway. No. 4 highway intersects more east and west highways in Saskatchewan than any other north and south highway. It intersects highways Nos. 32 , 40. 43 , 44, 51, 7, 13, 14 and 31, No. 5 to Lloydminster and Edmonton, and No. 26 west to St. WaLburg. The Montana state highway commission have determined on the location of a bridge in their area to be constructed across the Missouri river, and, if we had a bridge at Saskatchewan Landing we would, have then one of the best tourist roads from the United States to the national parks in the northern part of Saskatchewan. I mention this in order that it may be brought to the attention of hon. members as well as of the Minister of Labour, who foy this time I am sure is pretty well fed up with listening to representations from the member for Swift Current and others living in the district which would be served and benefited by that road.

speechtext: Not at all.

speechtext:
I am not able to say that any particular saving would result from its construction; the only saving would, be the elimination of the cost of the ferry.

But we should have much better traffic facilities for tourists from, the south, and this country has profited much from tourist traffic in recent years and is endeavouring to encourage it.
One of the objections to the building of this bridge has been that too large a part of the cost would go into- material and engineering and not direct relief. Well the material used has to come from its raw state at some stage and gives employment all along the line, even though it is not giving employment in the province in which the bridge is constructed. Of course it will give a considerable amount of employment there; it certainly is needed^ and it will give employment in other parts of Canada where steel, cement and other materials of the kind are produced. In addition I can say that the cost of the bridge will be materially lower than that of some other bridges which have been constructed, because of the fact that gravel and other materials are in close proximity.
An estimate has been made of the cost. The plans of the bridge have been prepared, and I understand that the provincial authorities are making representations to the dominion government for assistance in building it. I urge upon the minister and the government that an appropriation be made for this purpose at this session. The bridge is a sound undertaking; the cost is low, and the convenience to the public would be immeasurable.
I now come to another matter which it is somewhat foreign to my disposition to speak about; nevertheless I feel I should refer to it. The Minister of Finance in presenting his budget was able to give the people of this country a considerable amount of encouragement by reciting the progress which has been made and suggesting what may be expected in the future. I spoke a few minutes ago about the municipalities surrounding the area and the city which I happen to represent, and how well the people were satisfied with what is being done. I therefore dislike the sort of propaganda that is being put out through that district in order to foster discontent among the people. I refer to an article written by an hon. member of this house and published in a paper called The Advocate, in its issue of February 4. Because of the misrepresentations it contains it reflects upon every hon. member of the house and I feel that it should be brought to the attention of hon. members as well as of the country at large. I quote a portion of it:
For nearly three weeks we have bombarded the government benches with questions and

The Budget-Mr. Bothwell
accusations regarding the betrayal of the wheat board, the problems of the drought area, and the need for a peace program. Throughout the entire time not one Saskatchewan Liberal has opened his mouth although often invited to do so.
To-day there arose the matter of "gerrymandering" the constituencies for the next election. Immediately all the strong, silent men from Saskatchewan found their tongues. One after another they are rising and quibbling about the boundaries of their constituencies. Tempers flare and accusations fly back and forth.
Feeding, clothing, and caring for our people is of relatively little importance. Saving one's seat is of paramount importance. So this is parliament? Pardon me, I thought it was a kindergarten.
The heading of this is "Parliament from the Back Benches," by T. C. Douglas, M.P. That, Mr. Speaker, may be good literature but it does not state facts. I took occasion to check up Hansard after reading it, and I found that two members only from Saskatchewan spoke on this question when a motion was before the house in connection with redistribution. The matter was referred to the special committee on the elections and franchise acts, and only two members of the house from Saskatchewan who had reason to complain about the last redistribution took occasion to speak on it. But this article told the world:
Immediately all the strong, silent men from Saskatchewan found their tongues. One after another they are rising and quibbling .	. .
Feeding, clothing and caring for our people is of relatively little importance. Saving one's seat is of paramount importance.
I leave it to the house to judge as to the sincerity of the observation. I should like to read another paragraph from the same newspaper, The Advocate, of February 25, 1937. Speaking of the appropriation for defence purposes it says:
What makes it even more lamentable is when other members come to you afterwards and tell you that they feel the same way as you do but of course you understand it would not do for them to say anything.

The outstanding feature of the week was a very excellent speech by Hon. J. G. Gardiner, on the rehabilitation of the drought area. And listen to this:

Whereupon the Conservative leader laid him across the table and spanked him soundly, while Mr. Dunning looked on with a rather embarrassed expression on his face.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. member mind telling us what was said about the wheat board and the wheat question?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend can make his own speech. You see, he takes credit for being able to talk by the hour here; he says, "We bombarded the government for hours," but he might also tell the country that when the hon. member for Weyburn starts to talk there seems to be a sudden exodus in the direction of the corridors. If the speeches delivered by the hon. member in this house contain such misrepresentations as appear in his articles in The Advocate I can understand why that exodus occurs.
The other day the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) took exception to a question I asked of the hon. member for Qu'-Appelle (Mr. Perley). I thought he was very fair; he said:
I will admit that stereotyped resolutions emanating from some source or other were
sent to the farmers of western Canada, asking them to send in resolutions of that type...
I received several resolutions apparently of that type, all couched in pretty much the same terms. I attended only one of those meetings, and at it such a resolution was presented in typewritten form. I was there before the meeting was called to order. No resolutions committee was appointed; the audience was not asked to present any resolutions, and the only one that was brought before the meeting was the typewritten resolution. I am not going to labour the question; all the resolutions I received were not in exactly the same terms, but they followed the same form so closely that
The Budget-Mr. Bothwell

I agree with the hon. member for Macleod that a great many of these resolutions emanated from some source, and the farmers were asked to pass them and send them on.
The other day the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) twitted some hon. members of the house on their claim to fame based on the fact that they voted against the empire agreements in 1932. Well, Mr. Speaker, I have to plead guilty, if that is the correct term, to that offence, if it was an offence, of voting against the empire agreements at that time, and I am prepared to justify my action at any time. Under similar circumstances I would do the same thing over again. At that time we had the opportunity to compare the empire agreements with the Dunning budget of 1930, and there were so many differences that it was pretty hard for the people then sitting to the left of the Speaker to support the empire agreements. Personally I am convinced that the system of bargaining adopted in 1932 was not in the best interests of either Canada or Great Britain, and I believe the budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) in 1930 was greatly to be preferred.
I should like to compare the agreements of 1932 and the budget of 1930 for a few moments, before I discuss the new agreements. Under the Dunning budget there were 414 reductions in duty out of some 514 changes. Under the conference agreements there were 132 reductions out of 223 changes; fifty-five per cent in the latter case and eighty per cent in the former case. Under the Dunning budget the reductions were so generous as to render certain a substantial increase in imports. Under the conference agreements the reductions were so slight as to leave the rates almost prohibitive. Under the Dunning budget the reductions were made principally on goods in general use by practically all consumers. Under the conference agreements the reductions were principally on goods imported by manufacturers for further processing or on raw material, and it is quite arguable that those reductions would not be passed on to the consumer. Under the Dunning budget reductions on goods imported for direct sale to consumers were largely on the necessities of life and the implements of production. Under the conference agreements the reductions on goods imported for direct sale to consumers were largely on non-essentials, such as automobiles, sporting goods, perfumery, expensive linens, kid gloves, omnibuses, typewriters, and so on. Under the Dunning budget all reductions were based on the low Liberal tariff schedules of 1929. Under the

conference agreements the reductions were based upon the 1930 tariff increases plus the 1931 increases, both of which were very substantial. Under the Dunning budget excise taxes of Great Britain were not to be included when arriving at the cost for duty purposes. Under the conference agreements all costs including excise duties and exchange differentials were included in the cost for duty purposes. Under the Dunning budget the increases in duty number 100, out of a total of 514 changes, while under the conference agreement the increases in duty numbered 139 out of a total of 223. Under the Dunning budget the increases rarely applied to goods imported for direct sale to actual consumers. Under the conference agreement the increases chiefly applied to goods imported for direct sale to consumers. The Dunning budget deductions, according to Mr. Dunning's own words, were made "in the spirit in which we desire to meet all nations." The spirit of the conference agreement was clearly revealed by the right hon. the leader of the opposition, who said on October 12, 1932:
These agreements mark the first step forward in a definite scheme of closer empire economic association. They are based upon the principle enunciated by the Conservative party before the last election, and steadfastly supported by it from that time to the present.
That policy was further illustrated by observations appearing at page 900 of Hansard for 1932. The Dunning budget duty reductions were a generous gesture of good will to Great Britain, made in full assurance that they would meet with an equally generous response in the matter of increased purchases by her from Canada, and were unaccompanied by even the mildest rebuff to foreign nations. The conference agreements arrangements were the result of hard and fast bargaining, absolutely devoid of generosity or generous sentiment, accompanied by positive declarations of anti-foreign trade sentiment and distinctly anti-foreign tariff manipulations.

speechtext: Whose statement is that?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My statement. The Dunning budget tariff changes left Canada free to make similar or even greater reductions in duties on goods imported from foreign countries. The conference agreements bound Canada not to reduce existing duties on goods imported from foreign countries (a) on any of the 159 articles in the free list and (b) on 213 items and classes enumerated in schedule E of the agreement, if such action would reduce the margin of preference.
The Dunning budget proposals did not involve the idea of empire self sufficiency, or involve the exclusion of foreign nations. They

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
did not invite reprisals. On. the other hand the conference agreements were predicated upon the idea of empire economic selfsufficiency. Under the Dunning budget proposals, duties might be adjusted from time to time as experience required; they were not for any fixed term. Under the conference schedule the prescribed duties are fixed for five years certain.
Under the Dunning budget proposals the promotion of trade and the interests of the producer and consumer were the chief considerations. Under the conference agreements the manufacturer and the industrialist were clearly the chief consideration, with but little thought for the producer or consumer.

speechtext: What about the worker?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I now come to the agreement just negotiated with Great Britain, and appearing in the budget address of the Minister of Finance. I am not able to quote figures with authority, but from a study which has been made I believe my figures are approximately correct. Under the new agreement of 1937 approximately $300,000,000 worth of goods, based on the 1936 figures, are guaranteed continued free entry into the United Kingdom. Second, the margins between customs duties imposed by Great Britain on Canadian products and on products of other countries are definitely bound on articles of Canadian export, to an extent approximating $200,000,000 per annum.
People speak about concessions Canada has had to make. I do not believe they are concessions; it seems to me they are benefits. We are in a position to buy goods cheaper, and that should be a benefit to us rather than a concession granted to anybody else. On 179 items the British preferential tariff is reduced. Altogether 425 items are affected. On the remaining 246 items Canada has undertaken that the British preferential tariff shall not be increased during the lifetime of the agreement. Fixed margins are established on only 91 items, as against 215 in the trade agreement of 1932. On 21 of the 91 fixed margin items the measure of margin has been reduced. Sixty-nine textile items are involved in the new agreement, on 32 of which the preferential tariff has been lowered. Where specific duties occurred they have been reduced, and in others eliminated altogether. If cartels in the United Kingdom operate to the detriment of the Canadian consumer the preferential tariff on such cartel controlled articles may be suspended or modified. If after inquiry, it is established that Canadian manufacturers are found to be dumping goods 31111-99
into the British market, the Canadian government will remove the dumping restrictions against the same class of goods imported into Canada. Under the agreement we retain our ham and bacon quotas, and also maintain our position with respect to the export of Canadian cattle.
When we compare the new agreement with that of 1932 I submit there can be no question about the fact that our representatives brought back an agreement from Great Britain which will be of great value, and to a tremendous extent will benefit the Canadian consumer. I was deeply interested in an article appearing in the Financial Post, a copy of which I received on Saturday. It is a publication which has not always been favourable to this government, by any means.

They have set out four outstanding features of the new agreement with Great Britain, and there are one or two paragraphs in that connection I should like to read:
It is a great experiment: Attempting to maintain reciprocity with the United States, preferential trade with Great Britain and trade treaties with other countries, all alongside of each other. If Canada can make a success of the effort it will have shown the world the way to breaking down the barriers of extreme economic nationalism.
The treaty was by no means a simple thing to negotiate and its successful conclusion is a tribute to the patience and earnestness of Mr. Dunning. Mr. Runciman, Mr. Chamberlain and other cabinet ministers and governmental officials on both sides.
Throughout the article they draw attention to the fact that the new agreement will have the effect of benefiting the housewives in particular and the consuming public in general.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate on the budget speech may I first set out my general impressions of it, and secondly point out a major deficiency in it. Thirdly, may I indicate why the deficiency is there, how it could be remedied, and some reasons why I believe my remedy for it is sound.
For several reasons the minister's speech, in my opinion, deserves commendation. It manifested thoroughness, a literary standard of noticeably high quality,	optimism-much
needed at the present time-and enthusiasm, which is always to be appreciated in a speech of that kind. It encouraged and embodied lower duties, freer trade, wise protection, and the British preference. In my judgment, all these are sound for Canada.



The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
There was one thing with respect to trade which was omitted from the speech, greatly I think to its disadvantage. I think the time has come when we must look to a national board so to plan and manage our trade as to make sure some time beforehand that we shall not have adverse trade balances. Such a board was not provided.
In my opinion the speech deserves censure in that it states that the government is to depend entirely upon two sources for the money required, namely, taxation and borrowing. There are many people throughout the world inclined to condemn nationally created money, but they are going to find just as sure as they live that sooner or later they must subscribe to the principle of nationally created and issued money. The question is: Shall we build the bridge and cross it before we are thrust into the ditch?
Nationally issued money should have been used for many items. It should have been issued debt free and interest free, and it could have been so issued. There are many who are inclined to look with a certain amount of scorn upon this idea every time it is brought forward. For their benefit I should like to read a short quotation from a book by G. D. H. Cole, university leader in economics at Oxford, fellow of the University College at Oxford, vice president of the workers' educational association, vice chairman of the new Fabian research bureau, member of the economic advisory council. To make light of the opinion of such a man is a different thing from making light of the opinion of some upstart from Alberta.
These are his words:
Such a policy of government spending on public works is indeed the only way of making a larger supply of bank money effective in a situation in which private entrepreneurs find it more remunerative to leave productive resources unused. But, if this is to be the outcome^ why on earth should the government submit to pay interest for the privilege of borrowing resources which it has conferred the privilege of creating? Surely the right course is fox the government itself to create the money, paying no interest for its use, but limiting the amount created to the amount that the banks would be allowed to create in accordance with the principles of banking policy laid down earlier in this chapter.
The title of the book from which the above extract is taken is Principles of Economic Planning, and the extract is to be found at pages 113 and 114. This book was published in 1935, so we can be sure that the writer is familiar with conditions as they are to-day, not as they were twenty years ago, when many of the economic principles upon which we seem to be basing our procedure were laid down, principles which since that time have been found wanting.

There is a passage in the budget speech, to be found on page 1215 of Hansard, to which I should like to refer. It commences with the words "that the velocity of circulation" and continues to the words "advantageously produce." This passage merits special attention for it is here that the minister sets forth the economic theories upon which the budget is based. I should like to read short excerpts from this passage, and comment upon them as I go along. The first one is:
This indicates, Mr. Speaker, that the velocity of circulation of cheque-book money is speeding up with the rising tempo of business activity and the increase in public confidence.
I want to state definitely that the chequebook money referred to here is not the kind of money to which I was referring some time ago, nor is it the kind of money to which we of this group will be referring in the future. The passage continues:
This is the factor so frequently forgotten by advocates of monetary panaceas.
Note the scorn. Anything we propose is a panacea, not a suggestion. I believe the time has come in the history of this country when all parties should be prepared to go into a "huddle," to use an athletic expression, on our problems. If the united opinion of all can find a solution of our troubles, it will be greatly to our credit. Instead of that, any new suggestion is scouted as a panacea. I shall deal more particularly with panaceas in a moment or two. I quote:
The volume of money work done is the product of the amount of money multiplied by its velocity of circulation. An arbitrary increase in the amount of money by the fiat of a government is likely to defeat its object by a proportionate or more than proportionate decrease in the velocity factor.
It is just as likely to increase the velocity; that should also be noted. So much for that. Here is another excerpt:
If the increase in the volume of money continues beyond a certain but unpredictable point, public confidence is lost altogether and a flight from money occurs.
I submit that that point is unpredictable. How does the minister know that we are near the unpredictable point? How do the authorities who are managing the financial affairs of this dominion know that we are near that unpredictable point? I say that by no means are we near that unpredictable point. It has been said that if the increase in the volume of money continues, we will have a loss of public confidence; but may I say that if the decrease in the volume of money continues, we shall have a loss of

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
public confidence. In this case there will be a flight, not from money, but from goods, which would be just as disastrous. I quote again:
There will come a time, however, and it may come more quickly than many of us expect, when precisely the opposite policy will have to be followed, if the best interests of the country are to be served.
"Opposite" there meaning decreasing the amount of money. When that time comes we will crush even more the poor. What for? In order that we may be able to catch the few men who wish to speculate. Has the time not come when we should adopt some measure for controlling these speculators, rather than continuing to use vague and indefinite methods by which everyone in the country is ruined in order that the speculators may be caught? Again I quote:
But monetary policy should not be regarded as a panacea.
I submit that no social erediter regards monetary reform as a panacea. What right have opponents of social credit to dub it a "panacea"? The word panacea is used only by our opponents. Monetary reform has been desirable before now, but I submit that it is now essential if we are to deal in any effective manner with our problems of debt, of unemployment, of social service and of defence. This monetary question reminds me of the question of irrigation. When you have a wide semi-arid area of land on which people can no longer live, you begin to wonder whether you cannot find water to go on that land. Those who would advocate irrigation know full well that weeds will grow much more abundantly than before when irrigation is provided; that likewise there are dangers of flooding and water-logging and drowning crops, increasing the difficulty of the work and running up the overhead; the need for a new crop, such as sugar beets, to come in, and the alkali problem besides. But the point is this; they know very well they cannot live in the area unless they get the water. We are rapidly approaching the time, indeed we have reached it, when no longer in this Canada of ours can people live unless the money is available. It is not a question of calling the cure a panacea. Who calls the water used in an irrigation project a panacea? It is merely a sine qua non, to use the Latin expression, "without which nothing" you cannot live unless you get it. Here is another passage from the minister's speech.
It can at best only create conditions favourable to sound development. In a constructive program it should merely take its place as part of a much larger whole.
31111-99}
That statement is absolutely correct. No one from this group has ever contended anything else. But money is lacking among the people. Conditions are now unfavourable to this sound development. Just for an example, let a man go out and, become a farmer and try to get a line of credit without which he cannot possibly produce; he simply cannot get the line of credit. And that situation is multiplied ten thousand throughout this country. In another passage the minister says:
Fundamentally our need is an increase in our aggregate national income.
We all grant that. But how are you going to get it? Where in this budget speech has any indication been given as to how that thing is to be done? May I draw to the attention of the house something I have cited once before, a statement by Robert H. Hemphill, a prominent authority of the United States, to the effect that for every three dollars of income which the people of a country are going to have, there must be one dollar in circulation-not in the banks nor in the hands of wealthy men, but in circulation. It does not say that we are to have one dollar's worth of goods. Certainly we must have the goods, but goods without the tickets are not enough. We have money now, it is true; much of it, but it is in the hands of a few people from whom we find it impossible to get it away. What chance have the half million unemployed, their children and dependents, of getting any of that, money? Is it not, Mr. Speaker, as though you had plenty of blood, in your body but were unable to get it circulating in your hands and feet? What good, is the blood if it is not circulating?
Another passage from the minister's speech:
[DOT]-an increase in material wealth, not a different yardstick by which to measure it. Real purchasing power consists in goods and services produced, not in the number of monetary tickets which are used to facilitate the exchange of these goods and services.
This statement is a major error, as I am going to show as I go on with my speech. Meanwhile, will anybody prove that the tickets are not the thing that count? Will anyone tell me why it was that we had so disastrous a fall in the value of all manner of goods and property in 1929? If it was not that the tickets had been withdrawn, what was it? We still had the goods, but we called those goods in 1929 over-production, although no one had thought of calling them over-production before. Why the change? Values in the United, States fell two hundred billions of dollars. Why did that occur if

The Budget-'Mr. Blackmore
tickets made no difference? Was it because of lack, of goods? It was because of lack of tickets-these very things that are so scornfully disregarded.
What then makes purchasing power? We grant that an increase in material wealth comes first. We now have this wealth in abundance, and what abundance we have not [DOT] now we can easily get.
May I draw to the attention of the house a speech delivered by the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Kuhl) on March 3 as an indication of our possibilities with regard to goods. Why not have the tickets now if we can so easily get the goods-and we have them? The last passage to which I am going to refer is this one:
An increase in our national wealth and income can best be secured by facilitating the production of the many things which Canada is best fitted to produce and by exchanging these products on as large a scale as possible for products which Canada cannot advantageously produce.
I am going to challenge first of all the use of the word "best"; it needs to be qualified considerably. The general statement of the passage is good, but how this thing is to be brought about is the question. It is very much like the promises to which the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) referred, which the Liberals so freely and abundantly made. They were going to do all these things, but they knew not how. What is the use of telling what ought to be if you have no suggestion as to how the thing can be brought about? If the loss of tickets caused, all this trouble, why should we not now, by a discreet renewal of these tickets, remove the trouble we have had?
Turning from a consideration of the minister's speech let me go on to the reason why these difficulties have arisen as mentioned in the speech. It must be re-stated over and over again to hon. members that we have passed from one state of civilization to another; that we are trying to make a system which was satisfactory in the old situation fit the conditions of the new; and it certainly cannot be done. The minister defined purchasing power in a way which led to a great absurdity in his speech. He said that goods and services are purchasing power. Will hon. members pardon me while I examine that proposition for a few minutes. If goods and services are purchasing power, why is not the merchandise in a store purchasing power? Why do we have fire sales and clearance sales to raise money if the goods themselves are purchasing power? How about the cattle and swine and machinery and wheat that we had in such superabundance in 1932? If they were purchasing power, why were we not well off?

Again, if goods are purchasing power why a re we concerned about having dump duties to prevent the other fellow from giving us his goods, his purchasing power? Again, if goods are purchasing power, why are we so franctically eager to export our goods, beef and wheat and the like, which we so much need?
The final test whether goods and services are purchasing power is this. Will the government of this country part with one of its bonds for goods and services-coal, for example, or wheat or beef or wool? Of course it will not; the recognition of which fact is recognition of the fact that the definition which the minister has given of purchasing power is false.
Now, goods should be purchasing power; but they are not; they are merely potential purchasing power. The Liberals realize that; else why the anxiety for foreign markets? Selling bacon to Britain simply brings us British purchasing power-that is why we sell it there. It brings us their purchasing power, what we call money-their credit or foreign exchange; and with that thing, whatever we call it, we can buy machinery or anything else that we need. Therefore purchasing power is not goods and services; it is the thing for which we exchange goods and services. Some will say, " Well, you can trade bacon for clothes.1' Quite so. But according to the minister's definition clothes in Canada are purchasing power. But so is bacon. Then if we trade bacon for clothes we are merely trading purchasing power for purchasing power, a thing about as wise as trading one dollar bill for another dollar bill. Does that make anything like sense?
Worse still, we all know-members on the Conservative side particularly know very well, and so do the Liberals-that if clothes in Canada are purchasing power and you bring in too many British clothes your clothes in Canada are no longer purchasing power. That is a very serious matter. The members of this house can all clearly see the morass of difficulties into which that definition of purchasing power leads when you follow such a will-o'-the-wisp, for a definition of that sort is a will-o'-the-wisp and nothing else. Take some of our own contentious points that will arise in this house from time to time. We have sugar which we produce in Canada; it ought to be purchasing power, but it is not unless we can sell it. We want to sell it in Canada and therefore we try to exclude outside sugar, and thus we get into difficulties with the maritimes; for they, I understand, have potatoes and salt fish which should be purchasing power, but which are not unless they

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
can sell them. And they want to sell them exactly to the place that wants to sell sugar to us. Again we have manifest evidence that this definition is all wrong.
What has caused this error and consequent absurdity? I should like to speak very slowly and very earnestly to the members of the house on this subject, because right here we find the cause of our whole misconception. The budget speech is (based upon the theories and conceptions of the old economics. The guiding principle of the old economics, or the economics of scarcity, was this-mark the words-" Supply creates its own demand." These are not my words; they are the words of an eminent authority. " Supply creates its own demand." Let me read the words of one of the great teachers, John Stuart Mill, and see how nearly the minister's definition conforms to Mill's statement:
What constitutes the means of payment for commodities is simply commodities.
Good enough, but it leads to all the absurdities I have pointed out. Further:
Could we suddenly double the productive powers of the country, we should double the commodities in every market; but we should, by the same stroke, double the purchasing power. Everybody would bring a double demand as well as supply; everybody would be able to buy twice as much, because everybody would have twice as much to offer in exchange.
That was sound enough until we got into the era of overproduction; but everybody recognizes now that it is no longer sound. It is a little sounder than the minister's definition, but I will not take time to go into that now.
Here is a comment by John Maynard Keynes on that statement-and Keynes is recognized as an authority worth listening to. He says:
If this be true, then there is no obstacle to full employment.
Everybody sees the absurdity of that. Keynes leaves it at that, with impressive silence. At another point he says:
Professional economists after Maltahus were apparently unmoved by the lack of correspondence between the results of their theory and the facts of observation-a discrepancy which the ordinary man has not failed to observe, with the result of his growing unwillingness to accord the economists that measure of respect which he accords to other groups of scientists whose theoretical results are confirmed by observation when applied to facts.
That is exactly the trouble with us to-day. We simply cannot understand existing conditions because our conceptions were framed on the theories of the old economics; and as long as we continue to keep those old theories we shall be unable to explain the facts of the existing situation, and we shall never find a
solution. The definition is utterly unsound to-day because we are in an age of abundance, an age of technological unemployment, an age of high specialization. A hundred years ago a man made a pair of shoes with his own hands and could exchange it for a tin kettle if he wished. To-day if he were working in a factory and putting on heels on shoes, how could he exchange the act of putting heels on shoes for a kettle? That is a question that reveals in another aspect the absurdity of the whole situation which has developed from the ideas of the old economics.
We must have a new concept, for the old theories have become unsound because, as I say, we are to-day living in an age of plenty. Everyone knows that. As a simple illustration may I refer to page 42 of Howard Scott's Introduction to Technocracy. He there informs us that we have learned now to create a machine which has nine million times the working power that one human being has, and he says that 8,766,000 of these units have been developed since 1900. Must it not be manifest to any hon. member who thinks about the situation that there has been a great transformation which is absolutely epochmaking and which demands treatment that is revolutionary? The machine has displaced more and more men and will continue to do so in spite of everything we can do, as the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deach-man) pointed out so well the other night. We are living now in a time when we must acknowledge the new economics; otherwise we shall go on to our doom. We can laugh and sneer about it all we like, but we shall simply be marking time and deceiving the people while civilization crashes into ruin, and then we shall have the melancholy satisfaction of remembering that the danger was pointed out in time for us to have saved the situation if only we had been open-minded enough to see the new economics instead of lingering behind in the old. The new economics can be put in these words: Demand creates its own supply. Just the reverse of the old definition. For example, if you have money in your pocket, is there anywhere in Canada where you cannot get almost anything you want? The goods are here in abundance; what is needed is effective demand. What is effective demand? Effective demand is nothing more or less than those tickets which the minister so scornfully swept away, that is "monetary ti-ckes used to facilitate the exchange of goods and services."
Now what are the principles of these new economics? They are mainly three: (1) that the state shall create and issue the tickets, in the form either of pocketbook money or

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
cheque book money (2) that the state shall distribute this money, not leaving it to the banks, or to people or industry to borrow it; it must distribute the money itself, for public works, for defence, for social services such as pensions to ex-service men, to the aged:, to mothers, to the blind, and to unemployables, for the endowment of universities and schools, or by other means tending to bring about adequate use of our resources both material and human. To this end1 it may be necessary even to resort to dividends, that idea at which so many people are laughing uproariously. But why not dividends, first to supplement the low wages which men are receiving in industry, where they are often so painfully underpaid that they are suffering and driven to strikes? Or why not dividends for those for whom we can no longer find employment?
Then (3) There must be control of prices and prevention of inflation, by means of a device or mechanism called the just price. I have not time to talk about this in any detail, but those who see in the new economics a danger of inflation must be informed that there is a device in the social credit proposals which prevents inflation directly and scientifically, which device is called the just price and the compensated price. Much of this, of course, will have to be accomplished by cooperation with the provinces, but if this government can force certain provinces to accept a loan council in order to get money it ought not to be very difficult to use the monetary power to force them to do pretty nearly anything.
What grounds have we for believing that the new economics is sound? First, it harmonizes with facts as they are. Secondly, it would result in greater production of goods and in the extension of markets at home and abroad. Third, it could be managed so as to prevent inflation; and fourth, we have competent and responsible authorities who favour the acceptance of its principles. Among these are Professor G. D. H. Cole, and also Professor R. F. Irvine, for twenty-five years professor of economics in the university of Sydney, Australia, who makes the positive declaration that social credit is not only sound but is the only way to keep western civilization from being wrecked utterly.
Since the creation, issue and control of money, both pocket book and cheque book money, especially the latter, in an age of plenty such as is ours, possessing an abundance of goods and services, able to produce more abundantly, will turn these goods and services into actual purchasing power; and since

suoh creation, issue and control will bring about immediately much more goods, both producers' and consumers', which goods, according to the minister's own definition, are purchasing power; and since the best evidence tends plentifully to show that the age of scarcity has given place to an age of abundance ; and since an economic system of scarcity is obviously likely to be disastrous to an age of plenty; and since there are throughout Canada ghastly evidences that our present economic system has produced and is producing disastrous results; and since a great and growing body of informed opinion, supported by concurrence of an increasing number of highly respectable authorities, is convinced that creation and issue of government money in a country of plenty such as Canada, can be controlled so that it will not cause inflation or other destructive results, and offers the only possible Way out of an otherwise apparently hopeless situation, I once more respectfully urge the government to take immediate steps towards the introduction into Canada at an early date of the principles of the new economics, commonly called social credit, exercising the state's constitutional right and duty to create and regulate national money. The government of Canada will thus use the only effective means of dealing with the unemployment problem.
Even without exercising that right the government in 1936-37 could in some measure have alleviated unemployment if it had dealt otherwise with the marketing of Canadian wheat. The evidence indicates strongly that the government's policy deprived the prairie farmers of many millions of dollars in this year of most urgent need. And every dollar lost to the farmer deprived him of a dollar's worth of necessities, deprived Canadian industries of a dollar's worth of sales, deprived the Canadian government itself of revenue from tariff and sales tax, added to the burdens of the provinces and municipalities, and rendered the debt situation more intense.
Therefore, as a representative of a great farming constituency and a great farming province I feel it my duty to move an amendment to the amendment, as follows:
And that this house also regrets the action of the government in passing order in council P.C. 2202, which in effect deprived western farmers of the privilege of selling wheat to the wheat board unless the price of wheat dropped below 90 cents per bushel for wheat graded as No. 1 northern at Fort William.
