speechtext:
But I can assure the hen. gentleman that if he inquires in the man-times to-day about the price of potatoes he will be assured that potatoes are purchasing power, because they bring a nice penny.
First, I wish to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) on his splendid presentation of the budget. It is not often that I do that, but he has made an admirable presentation. I was disappointed, however, that I and my colleagues who are associated in the business world obtained no relief from certain nuisance taxes that have bothered us for several years; that there was no reduction in the sales tax, and that the minister did not find it possible to eliminate the sugar tax entirely, which I think would have pleased everybody in the country. I was glad to see the minister in the house this afternoon, and to learn that he had recovered from his illness. I hope he will find it possible to be in the house constantly from now on, because I like the twinkle in his eye when things are going his way, and sometimes the scowl on his face when things are going the other way.
I do not intend to take up the time of the house in ipresenting a great many figures, but I should like to make some general observations particularly with regard to what took place in this country from 1921 on, after the Liberal party came into power. I think it was the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) who said that any government could eliminate unemployment if it went the right way about it. That is not my view; I do not think any government can end unemployment without the cooperation of the rest of the world. I do not think the present government can be expected to end unemployment, which they did so much to create from 1921 to 1930 by meddling with business and tariffs. I contend that that administration fell down on the job, and caused unemployment at a time when the country was or should have been prosperous. There is no doubt in my mind that our lack of prosperity was due in large part to governmental interference with business and tariffs.
At that time the United States caused most of our difficulties, and no attempt was made by the Liberal party to formulate a policy for Canadians. They seemed to be afraid of offending our neighbours to the south. My own view as that if we had looked after ourselves they would have admired us more. The Fordney-McCumber tariff, which was introduced in the United States in 1921, 1922 or 1923-I do not remember the year but I remember what happened-practically shut out all farm produce that previously had been imported into the United States. I remember it so well because at that time I was exporting a great many cars of mixed vegetables, turnips and so on. That tariff imposed duties so high that it was impossible to ship anything to the United States. As a rule there are no customs houses in the interior of that country, and we who were shipping turnips and other vegetables had to buy the commodity, pay the duty and sometimes pay the freight as well. That was too great a risk to take in shipping vegetables down through Virginia and that section of the United States. Incidentally there is one example in the United States that might be followed by this country. We have too many customs houses in the interior of Canada; I think a great many of them could be closed. We had to clear everything through Black Rock or Niagara Falls, and no
The Budget-Mr. Spence

one in the business could afford to take the chance, because at that time the duty was higher than the price of the commodity we were shipping.
Then in 1930 the Hawley-Smoot tariff worked a great hardship on the dairying interests of Canada, who were entirely shut out of the American market. No effort was made by the party then in power to work out a policy for Canadians. Before the Conservative party came into office in 1930 Canada had lost her world markets; there were a great many unemployed in the country; the balance of trade was against us, and we landed in an awful mess. The party now in power had continued to interfere with tariffs and the business world until the investing public became discouraged. We have failed to restore the confidence of the investing public, and until we do that I do not see any hope of curing unemployment.
Hon. members will remember when we first reduced the tariff on farm implements around 1924 or 1925. At that time the Massey-Harris people were located in the end of my riding. They increased the size of their plant in Batavia, New York, and did all the work possible there. Then they shipped their goods to ithe northwest from Batavia instead of from Toronto. In those days the Massey-Harris Company employed people by the thousand where now they employ them by the hundred. I remember when the streets surrounding the Massey-Harris plant were black with people coming out at five o'clock in the evening, but that is not the case today, and I have no doubt that some of the negotiations carried on by the administration then in power were responsible for a good deal of that employment. To-day in Canada thousands of people have plenty of money to invest, but they are encouraged to invest it only in government bonds, which to my mind simply ties up money and keeps it away from business and industry. That is so simply because the people feel that government bonds are the only safe investment. Even to-day, though the interest on bonds is very low, investors consider them much safer than other investments. I have had some experience in the business world and in industry, Mr. Speaker, and I know of nothing that will do more to create employment than encouraging the investor to put his money into industry. Then the government should leave industry alone-stop interfering with it.
The closing of the relief camps, which the government tried to make us believe would be to the advantage of the young men in the camps brought no improvement at all. The

men who were taken out of those camps and put to work put others out of employment, as I think was said by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) the other day. The government simply put one class of people out of employment and gave work to others. As I understand it, some camps are open to-day. They may not be under the regulations of the federal government or under the Department of National Defence as they were formerly, but this government must remain responsible for their upkeep. Those camps served a useful purpose, and may I say they were started by a man with a big heart, Hon. Donald Sutherland, for the purpose of giving these young men something to do, good beds to sleep on, good food to eat and plenty of clothing. If it had been possible to keep out the agitators all would have been well, but those agitators were encouraged by speeches made in this house. Otherwise there never would have been any difficulty and the government would not have had to interfere at all.
There is another thing for which I suppose I can hardly blame the Liberal party entirely, but as a rule they always employ the wrong men to carry on investigations. I am sorry to say that sometimes, but not very often, we have done the same thing. For instance, when it was suggested to build up a business in the West Indies, an hon. member of the house who knew nothing about goods produced in Jamaica or any part of the West Indies, was appointed to go there. He came back with a wonderful report, talking about picking beautiful, juicy oranges off the trees, and about the grapefruit of the West Indies, which even to-day are not considered of any great value when compared with the product of Texas or Florida. His glowing report succeeded in convincing the then government that in the West Indies we would find a great market for our products. I believe he stated that we would send them large quantities of flour and lumber. As a result a steamboat service, which has cost this country hundreds of thousands of dollars, was established. That was a foolish thing for the government to do.
Mr. Black, who at that time was senior member for Halifax, was interested in the steamboat business, because he had boats running to the West Indies and other ports. On that occasion he advised strenuously and vigorously against the service, but despite his efforts the government carried on and established a steamboat route which has lost lots

The Budget-Mr. Spence
of money. No young country can stand maladministration of that kind. The merchant marine of that day was losing plenty of money, without our establishing any such service.
Investigations of one kind and another have been carried on, all of which have proved failures. The present invesigation into the textile business is political, so far as I can see, and a regular pork barrel. Counsel for the commission, Mr. McRuer, has spoken for three weeks, stopping only to sleep and eat; God knows how much he is getting per day.

The National Employment Commission was another unfortunate move on the part of this government, one which is costing the country a large amount of money. When the measure setting up the commission was before the house I fought it vigorously, on the ground that we were creating another big spending department, like the civil service commission. All the commission has done has been to repeat the work of obtaining statistics which were already in the office of the Department of Labour. I am going to say one kind word to my hon. friends to my left. They are always ready to advocate impossibilities. They are always ready to blame bad times on the government in power. I claim that no government can bring about prosperity, but we should have an economic administration which we are not getting to-day, to help bring back prosperity.
I come now to the vegetable oil situation, to which some hon. members have referred already, and. about which I believe I know something. It has been discussed by the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris), who knows the business well and thinks of his fellow men. It was also discussed by the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Thompson), who is a successful farmer and knows what he is talking about. I hope the government will heed their advice and protect Canada's dairy industry, which is one of her chief interests. If they do not it is my belief that with vegetable oils coming in as rapidly as they have done during the past three years, dairying will be practically ruined in another two years. The subject has been before the tariff board, and we have been expecting its decision for some time. I hope the government will try to influence the tariff board, if they need any influence.

While Canada is a great country for mines and minerals and forests and water power, it has also great opportunities for hunting and fishing which attract tourists, and I suggest to the government-

speechtext:
If the hon. member wants to make a speech, let him get up after I have finished. When I was interrupted I was referring to the importance of catering to the tourist trade. In some way it should be made clear to those who cater to this trade that the government desires them to treat their guests with the greatest courtesy. Nothing will bring the tourist back faster than pleasant memories of his treatment at summer resorts. I am sorry to say there are some places where the people endeavour to take all the gold they can out of the tourists. At the present time we spend through the Canadian National about $200,000 a year to induce vacationists to come to this country. Perhaps if we treated these tourists in the way I have suggested, all or much of this $200,000 might be saved. It is just a suggestion; I am never opposed to spending money to make money, and I do not object to the appropriation of $200,000.
A great deal has been said in this house about our foreign markets. No doubt at times they are a real necessity, but it should not be forgotten that export trade may be cut down or cut off at any time through competition from other countries. So, I say, we must have more people. Some hon. members will not agree with this point of view, but I have given it a great deal of study, and in my opinion we need more people to consume our products, thus furnishing a stable market. My personal views are that we should admit into Canada all the British and Scandinavian immigrants who will come in under their own steam. One 
will make work for the other. Labour leaders may not agree with me, but I cannot agree with them all the time. In this vast area we have lots of room for more people.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about the hundreds of thousands who are unemployed and on relief?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We will make work for them by bringing in another million people. It looks selfish not to fill the vacant spaces which we have in this country. Some other nation may have its eye on these opportunities. I name no names, but such things might happen in these days when so many international difficulties arise. I should like the government to consider allowing British and Scandinavian immigrants to come into the country.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext:
If they do not adopt this policy now, they will have to do so later. It would take forty million people to do justice to this country. Eleven millions cannot carry the burden any longer-and that, or probably a little less, is our population to-day. An increased population would solve our transportation problems and benefit the country in a variety of ways. I know that on this subject I differ from some of my friends, but perhaps I have a vision of the future which some others do not share. I hold that this country will not regain prosperity until our population is much greater than ten millions. Sir John A. Macdonald and his associates thought that they had achieved a wonderful success when they brought about confederation, but lately it has been more difficult than ever before to hold confederation together. Canada is a vast country where different interests must be served. What suits the extreme east does not suit the extreme west, and what is acceptable to both extremes does not suit the centre. As far as I can see, there is no hope that a zone tariff could be arranged to regulate commodities and be fair to all parts of the country.

More were started in that
time than in any other period in the history of Canada, at any rate as far as I can remember. For example, -take Canadian Industries Limited, which controls fifty per cent of the factories in the country. When anyone thinks that he is buying from an individual factory to-day and discovers that in all probability he is buying from Canadian Industries Limited, he is disappointed. We find that Canadian Industries Limited is controlled by the du Pont people of New York. I would suggest to the government that this sort of thing should be curbed so as to allow the small industries, and business houses, to get a chance, and have the profits remain in Canada. As things are they are leaving Canada to-day, the money being made by American concerns. Soon the United States will have the country iby purchase, and what will Canadians say then, when this North American continent may be all one country?
In my opinion, the government made a mistake when they changed the wheat board. Mr. McFarland and his associates did good work, for Mr. McFarland proved that he was a good manipulator. He had an advisory board of eight, four representing the railways and industrial concerns, the other four being farmers. No doubt the farmers should have some say in regard to the disposition of wheat. However, that has all been explained by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) and I will not go over it again. Now we have Mr. Murray at the head of the board, with Mr. Mclvor-they cannot do without him because he provides some of the brains for the board -and A. M. Shaw, a man so full of education that his brains probably cannot contain any practical ideas; and on top of that we have an advisory committee composed of four ministers of the crown. Who can say that this is not a political wheat board? I am not condemning the ministers because they are all capable of serving on any board, but it seems hardly fair to the farmer, who I think has been sold out.
The rehabilitation bill was brought into the house a few days ago, and in that regard I may say that we in the east are willing to make some sacrifices in order to rehabilitate western Canada. But it makes it difficult for us to assist them when three or four members from that locality will get up and abuse the east for criticism of the west, suggesting that we have no consideration for the people in that part of Canada. Let me assure you, Mr. Speaker, that in my own riding I have
been criticized repeatedly on account of the money spent in the west. I submit, therefore, that it would be better if we did not have such speeches from hon. members. When the vote is going their way, it is not necessary to let the whole world know what we are doing in this house. I am willing to do whatever I can in my own small way to help to hold confederation together. Winston Churchill once said that the curse of the world has been the aggressive socialist movement, which is the enemy of ordered liberal progress in any country, and so I say, Mr. Speaker-and I am going to cut my remarks very short-that we- should get together, become acquainted, be good friends with one another, and cooperate as far as we can and encourage cooperation with other countries; because no nation can live to itself and be successful.
Those are my views and I thank the house for the patient and attentive hearing I have had. I appreciate the fact that I have not done justice to the speech I intended to make, but that is because I have not been feeling as well as I should like to, and perhaps I should never have started at all.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In the dinner hour I looked up the Rules and Forms and I find that rule [DOT]422, page 131, says:
The law on the relevancy of amendments is that if they are on the same subject matter with the original motion, they are admissible, but not when foreign thereto. The exceptions to this rule are amendments on the question of going into supply or ways and means.
That is the broad general statement of the situation, but the question of relevancy has always been held to be one of importance in dealing with a matter of this kind, and where an entirely new matter is added by the use of the word "also," it falls within the general rule. I mentioned that the rule apparently contemplated the possibility of amendments being moved after the amendments before the chamber had been disposed of. Rule 423 says:
When a motion, an amendment and an amendment to the amendment have been proposed, the speaker will first take the sense of the house on the last by saying: "Is it the

The Budget-Speaker's Ruling
pleasure of the house to adopt the amendment to the amendment?" After this has been disposed of, another may be moved as soon as the Speaker has proposed the question: "Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the amendment (or the amendment as amended) to the main motion?" After this has been disposed of, the Speaker will propose: "Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion (or the motion as amended) ?" Then a member may move another amendment. Any number of amend-nents may be proposed in this way.
On going into supply there is of course a limitation to this procedure by the practice of parliament. The rule was laid down, by Mr. Speaker Lemieux, I believe, that only what amounts to an amendment to the amendment might be moved. This, of course, is a motion to go into ways and means, which presumably stands upon the same footing. As one of the authorities, I believe, puts it, by the law and custom of the constitution we have established. that principle. Standing order 49 says:
Only one amendment and one subamendment may be made to a motion for Mr. Speaker to leave the chair for the house to go into committee of supply or ways and means.
We are therefore subject to the limitation which is contained in that rule, and the general principle that any number of amendments can be moved, which I mentioned before recess, would be an erroneous statement of the situation. There can be only one amendment and one amendment to the amendment when it is a motion to go into supply or ways and means; but if it is a motion for second reading, or any other resolution, when the house has disposed of the first subamendment and then the amendment, it is competent for any member who has not yet spoken to move any amendment that would be relevant, according to the rules as I understand them and as laid down in May, at any rate.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

I have looked into the matter, and I believe that the point of order is well taken. There must be some relation between an amendment and a subamendment; there must be some relevancy of the one to the other. In this instance the subamendment raises a new and quite different subject matter. Members of the house might be willing to vote for 
the amendment, but if you added this subamendment, which is another matter altogether, they might be opposed to the subamendment and would have no opportunity to express their views. The same applies to those who might be in favour of the subamendment, but not of the amendment. The subamendment must be relevant to the amendment, as amending the amendment. This subamendment does not amend the amendment; it simply *adds to it a different matter altogether.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
During the recess I had occasion to consult the notes of Hansard and I find that the point raised by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) had been well taken. I might refer the house to standing order 49 and to paragraph 394 of Beauchesne's Rules and Forms:
A motion may be amended: (a) by leaving out certain words; (b) by leaving out certain words in order to insert other words; (c) by inserting or adding other words.
If we look at the amendment it does noit propose to follow that procedure at all, but dt is entirely a new motion. Paragraph 395 says:
It is an imperative rule that every amendment must be relevant to the question on which the amendment is proposed. Every amendment proposed to be made either to a question or to a proposed amendment should be so framed that if agreed to by the house the question or amendment as amended would be intelligible and consistent with itself.
I do not find that if this proposed amendment were allowed, it would make the amendment it is proposed to amend consistent with itself. Then further, in An Introduction to Procedure of the House of Commons, by G. F. M. Campion, we find on page 150 under the heading Amendments to Amendments the following:
An amendment to an amendment stands in the same relation to an amendment as an amendment itself does to a motion.
This is not in the form of an amendment to the main motion or in the form of an amendment 'to the amendment. If it be considered in relation to the motion it cannot be a subamendment, but it must be an amendment, and there is nothing on the face of it to show that it is intended to amend the amendment. Moreover, as the leader of the opposition ('Mr. Bennett) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) have stated, it does not deal with the same subject matter as the amendment. It is in my opinion foreign to the amendment submitted by the leader of the opposition, and I therefore have to declare it out of order.

The Budget-Mr. Fleming

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In rising to take part in this debate I do so with considerable trepidation; the subject is of such vast importance and can be approached from so many angles that it is difficult to decide which features to discuss. First, however, may I heartily congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) upon the splendid budget which he brought down, which will remain a memorable document among the public records of this country. No one will deny that the budget presented to this house was a bold budget, and that was expected from so courageous and aggressive a gentleman as the Minister of Finance. Those characteristics he exemplified when as Minister of Railways and Canals he changed the terminus of the Hudson Bay railway from Port Nelson to Fort Churchill. Western Canada will ever be grateful to him for that change and thank him for the tactful manner in which he pushed that railway project to a conclusion. When he presented his budget he showed those same qualities of courage and progressiveness, and again Canada should be grateful to him.
I intend to vote against the amendment and for the motion. In so doing I am confident that I express the opinion of the great majority of the people I have the honour to represent in this parliament. I favour the present budget because it is in accordance with Liberal policy, which has achieved such great successes throughout the length and breadth of Canada in recent years. I accept the budget because it is a Canadian budget, made in Canada to meet Canadian needs and the situation as it really exists in Canada at the present time. By degrees we are becoming more accustomed, to conditions to which we have been brought by the depression. Instead of blaming this one and that one at home we are beginning to realize that we belong to a world order and that our ups and downs are the result, not altogether of our own wise actions and our costly errors, but of the conditions that obtain elsewhere. To quote from the budget speech as reported at page 1211 of Hansard:
Viewing the situation broadly, however, in the light of the progress of the past year and the major underlying forces at work, I believe I can fairly say that since 1929 no New Year has dawned with brighter promise for Canada. I shall be greatly disappointed if. by this time next year, Canada had not moved substantially further along the road of economic recovery.
Those of us who a few years ago were so optimistic about the return of good times during an overnight sleep are now prepared to wait with the rest until the world has made a few more revolutions in its orbit. There is
no going ahead alone. If we raise more wheat than the world can buy we must store it or destroy it or use it for feed. If we build more railways than are necessary to carry our freight and passengers the rails will rust through disuse, and if they are national railways the nation must pay the price. If our factories turn out more goods than they can sell, they must close their doors and dismiss their employees. It will require the utmost wisdom to determine what the nation should do to maintain its place in the world of trade, and just as much wisdom to determine what producers in farm and factory should do to preserve the national equilibrium.
Here are some of the suggestions which have been made. A suggestion, of course, is not a solution; in nearly every case there are counter suggestions. Among the suggestions are these: produce less grain; raise more stock; produce more grain and keep the railways busy; produce less in the factories; give shorter hours to men; put the tariff up higher; lower the tariff to any country that will trade with us; stop immigration; fill up the prairies; bring more people into the country; spend; save; make war on Russia; copy Russia; get back to the simple life; break up machines and revert to hand labour; close the universities; cultivate trade within the empire; complete the lake route and get another means of transportation even though there is nothing to transport. And, above all, find fault with everyone who is trying to do something, and finally, if you are of good Canadian or British stock revile the foreign-bom. But we must always remember that epithets have no place in logic and will not help towards a solution.
Is there a solution? Must we admit that the human mentality is not capable of combating the forces at present striving to bring chaos into the world? I for one cannot resign myself to that view. I sincerely believe that there is a solution, and a clear-cut one. The solution as I see it is practicable even though it may not be immediate. As the stagnation of trade is a result of world conditions, the remedy is to be sought by bringing about better world conditions, a more friendly attitude and closer trade relations. If nations are bound to act as schoolboys with chips on their shoulders there will continue to be misunderstanding, aloofness and possibly war. But if the law of life, which makes each think of others as of self, is observed, it will not be long until there is concord and enduring peace. If along with good will there is a determined endeavour to break down barriers to trade and tariffs of exclusion, then each country will proceed to
The Budget-Mr. Fleming

give to the world what nature intended it to give, and will exchange its production freely for something which it needs but cannot advantageously produce or manufacture. Free trade and protection are not policies about which nations should wrangle, they are policies that must be faced and settled by the world at large, and their debating point is not in this capital city of Canada but at Geneva.
As to which policy should be followed, there is for me only one policy, the policy which this government has followed and which previous Liberal governments have followed in the past-the policy of the freest international exchange of commodities possible under existing conditions; the absence of artificial interference with international exchange, and the territorial division of industry with its resulting advantages. Its essence is perfect impartiality in the fiscal treatment of home and foreign products. It involves the removal of all artificial restrictions on, or encouragements to, particular industries. In free trade there are no differential duties, no bounties; taxation is for revenue only, and not for protection. It would appear, then, from consideration of the benefits to be derived from international trade that, from the cosmopolitan standpoint, that is, looking to the interests of the world as a whole, permanent protection is theoretically unsound. Temporary protection, however, might be justified in theory, on the ground, that it would enable some industry to secure a footing in a country where it was likely to thrive to the general benefit, or would prevent the transfer of an industry through temporary causes from a country otherwise specially suited to it. To render such temporary protection expedient in practice however, would involve on the part of men a degree of insight and foresight with which they are not generally credited. Hence I conclude that from the cosmopolitan standpoint free trade as a rule is, even in theory, and always in practice expedient.
From the national standpoint, however, the argument for free trade and against protection is more complicated. The parties to any act of exchange are in general not nations but individuals, and though both parties gain in utility from the exchange it does not follow that there is a gain to both the nations to which they respectively belong. There is no necessary harmony between the interest of the individual and that of the nation. This possible conflict of interests has been ignored by some dogmatic free traders but has been recognized by all leading English exponents of free trade principles from Adam Smith down to our day.

The most general economic argument in favour of free trade from the national standpoint is that protection, while it may benefit a particular home industry by attracting more capital into it, is yet injurious to the nation as a whole. Its primary object is to raise the price to the consumer who, therefore, is exploited in the interests of a small class of producers. Its effect is a less economic distribution of the nation's productive powers. The same labour and capital which would produce the protected article would find employment under a free regime in producing something else wherewith to buy directly or indirectly more of that article.
All trade is barter; exports pay for imports. The latter are really the reward for which the former are the necessary sacrifice; and we ought, therefore, to buy in the cheapest and sell in the dearest market. But while this argument in favour of free trade is in the main sound, it is easy to point to exceptional cases in which from the national standpoint a departure from free trade principles might be theoretically justifiable. For instance, (1) the validity of the " infant industry " argument for protection might be admitted in special cases; (2) on the ground of national independence, that defence is of much more importance than opulence, certain restrictions in trade may be advocated; (3) retaliation, but this act should be one of great deliberation. The crucial point is, are they likely to be successful in forcing the foreign nation to modify its hostile tariff or to abolish its export bounty, as the case may be?
Even in view of the above exceptions, it is well to remember that it is often a mistake to suppose, when some particular case has been discovered for which it is possible to find a theoretical justification for protection, that a departure from the broad principle of free trade, or taxation for revenue only is therefore desirable. The classical English argument against admitting exceptions to that principle is based not so much on the theoretical excellence of free trade as on the inherent weakness of governmental action; that is, on the practical difficulties in any conceivable system of protection and the abuses with which it is invariably associated. Protective duties, though few and small at first, tend to grow and spread, once the principle is admitted, until the outcome is a general high tariff-such a state of affairs as existed in Canada from 1930 to 1936 and in Great Britain prior to the reforms of Hutchinson, Peel and Gladstone.
It is well at this point to deal with the doctrine that restraint should be put on all articles imported from countries with which

The Budget-Mr. Fleming
the particular balance of trade is unfavourable. Whereas the protectionist policy has its origin in private interest and the spread of monopoly, these extraordinary restraints arise from national prejudice and animosity. Thus, for example, if free trade with France did lead to an unfavourable balance with France, it might yet render the true balance with the world more favourable in general to England. There is no certain criterion obtainable of the real balance between the home country and any other particular country.
The mercantilists supposed that in foreign trade what one country gained another lost, and that if the balance were even in value neither of them gained or lost. They looked on the question of the advantages of foreign trade as one of profit and supposed that this profit from the national point of view is measured by the amount of treasure received. In answer to this I will point out the real advantages of foreign trade:
1.	The real advantage is not merely profit and still less a balance of money, but a gain in productive power and utility. We may look at it more from the point of view of the producer than the consumer.
2.	(a) The country in the foreign trade of which there is the greatest proportion of native exports and the least of foreign reexports will be the chief gainer because there will be more employment for home labour and capital; (b) trade with a nearer country is more advantageous than with a remote one; (c) the richer neighbouring nations are the better. We gain not by making our neighbours poorer, but richer. They are thus better customers. One nation's loss is not another's gain, but, in general, a loss also.
It is becoming almost universally accepted that absolute free trade is practically impossible ; of necessity, then, it follows that the next best policy is that of reciprocity. Reciprocity is a question of mutual concessions in the matter of tariffs. It is the middle course between free trade and protection. In this case one country will agree to lower its duties on imports from another, or on some of them, provided that the second country in return will agree to lower its duties on its imports from the first country. There have been many objections hurled against the present government for its attitude on reciprocity treaties. The best argument against this attack is contained in the budget speech of the Minister of Finance. Speaking of the trade agreement with the United States, at page 1240 of Hansard, he said:
_ I am sure it will be a matter of special interest to the house to observe the growth in our trade with the United States, as we
now have a full year's experience under the operation of the agreement which established new schedules of rates on January 1, 1936. During the year our total trade with the United States, including commercial gold, amounted to $787,000,000 as compared with $683,000,000 for 1935, an increase of $104,000,000, or 15 per cent. If we exclude commercial gold entirely from the figures for the two years under comparison we find that the trade increase in 1936 was just over 22 per cent. Calculated on this same basis, exports to the United States were greater by 26 per cent, while imports from the United States were higher by 18 per cent. It will be noted that these percentage increases are appreciably above the corresponding increases in our trade with all countries. The increase in trade with our nearest neighbour is ample evidence of the benefits which follow a policy of seeking wider markets through trade agreements.
It would be impossible to claim that all of this price increase can be attributed to the trade pact between Canada and the United States, yet it certainly must have been one factor in improving the general price scale. The fact that the general world price level has risen must be considered as well. I can see only one reason for this advance, namely, the return to a freer passage of goods between the countries of the world. After about six years of the most nationalistic policies the world has ever experienced, most of the nations are returning to the policy of reciprocal treaties. That some are still adhering to the nationalistic policy of self-independence does not alter the fact that there is more freedom of trade now than existed last year or since 1928-29.
Since 1932-33, the low years of the depression, the world experienced a slow movement in the abolition of trade barriers, with the result 'that prices have increased, production has gone up in volume and the purchasing power of the people has risen. That the depression is vanishing is, or at least should be clear to all. The process, however, is slow, due mainly to the nationalistic tendencies of a few countries. There is nevertheless great hope that 'before long these nationalistic countries will realize the error of their ways. France underwent that change recently when her new government took office. Whether other nationalistic countries and one-man controlled countries can do the same without a major conflict is almost impossible to predict. Only when all the nations see clearly that to be prosperous is to be at peace can there be any real assurance of international stability and freedom of trade.
There are perhaps various ways in which world peace can be obtained, but I feel that the best -and surest way is by mutual concessions in trade relations, a more "give"

The Budget-Mr. Fleming

than the present "take" feeling. This is pointed out very well in the budget speech at page 1215 of Hansard:
. . . by exchanging these products on as large a scale as possible for products which Canada cannot advantageously produce. To these objectives the government has been energetically devoting itself by opening up and expanding foreign markets for our basic products, by stimulating employment in productive lines, and by endeavouring to eliminate uncertainty and fear which paralyze initiative and retard industrial enterprise. The success of these efforts is indicated in part at least-for I do not wish to claim for the government all the credit for the recovery which we have enjoyed.
We may, I believe, feel sure that if no major conflict arises in Europe or in the far east the nations will one by one follow that program, if for no other reason than that of self-preservation. No nation can be selfdependent or follow that policy for any length of time without grave danger to itself. Various nations in the past have felt the curse of this policy. More will feel it in the future if they continue their present nationalistic course.
It is, then, most essential that Canada should be prepared to cooperate in the common work of political appeasement and economic cooperation, and if this work is to succeed it needs the collaboration of all. If that collaboration is forthcoming there cannot be any doubt in the mind of 'anyone that we can create a better, saner and more prosperous world. We must learn the ways of economic cooperation so that the standards of life can be raised. We must never forget that our objective in Canada must be the prosperity of all. This point was brought out most strongly in the words of Anthony Eden when, speaking of Great Britain, he said:
We are willing to help toward a further advance along the line of increased economic opportunity, but this should be in our view on one condition. Economic collaboration and political appeasement must go hand in hand. If economic and financial accommodation merely result in more armaments and more political disturbance the cause of peace will be hindered rather than helped. On the other hand, new and freer economic and financial collaboration based upon solid, well conceived political undertakings will be powerful aid towards the establishment of unity of purpose in Europe. Ultimately and fundamentally the object of all honest political endeavour in whatever country must be a raising of the standard of life. We know well enough from the resources of science to-day that can be done, if it is undertaken in an atmosphere of peace and mutual confidence.
Consideration of the raising of the standard of life brings us to another exceedingly important point. It is freely admitted that we are entering the period of recovery. I feel

it my duty to congratulate the Minister of Finance upon the warning he gave the Canadian people when he said, as reported at page 1217 of Hansard:
It may seem ironical for me to sound a warning about a problem of prosperity whilst we are still harassed by the problems of depression. Evidence is accumulating however, of the prevalence of a state of mind which justifies a -warning signal. If we may judge by the activity in brokerage offices, the rapid rise in stock-market prices, and the ratio of stock prices, particularly in some sections of the market, to nearby earnings and dividend prospects, we are forced to recognize a revival of that get-rich-quick spirit which proved so disastrous in the pre-depression years.
However, I would1 urge the government to do its utmost to prevent a disaster similar to the one we experienced in 1929. Between 1923 and 1929 on an unparalleled scale, banks united, especially in the United States, in financing speculation, in securities and real estate. Comparatively little of the huge expansion of bank credit was utilized in financing an expansion in the physical volume of industry and trade. The process involved the tying up of a larger and larger proportion of bank funds in assets of a non-liquid character. The investments of the banks and the collateral they accepted for loans consisted1 of securities and real estate, capitalizing at an unreasonable rate the high earnings of business concerns enjoying a temporary and unstable prosperity at the expense of other elements of the population and business world.
On the average, the farmers' purchasing power during the depression period was more than ten per cent less than it would have been if the 1909-14 parity of prices had prevailed. This was bad -enough, but to make matters worse taxes on farm property during this whole period remained on a level ranging from 246 per cent to 267 per cent of the pre-war level, and almost twice as high as the price of farm products, relative to the pre-war level. Naturally the farmers' power to buy and pay for products of industry was severely curtailed, even in the absence of heavy mortgage and interest payments hanging over from the period of wild speculation in farm land during the land boom of 1919 and 1920.
It was only a matter of time until such artificial prosperity must collapse, the bubble of speculation would be pricked, and the banks would be hard put to it to realize in full on their assets. Forced liquidation on an unheard of scale could easily have been predicted by any well trained banker or economist familiar with the facts and capable of reasoning without bias. Such predictions, in fact, were not lacking, but they were unpopular and

The Budget-Mr. Fleming
unheeded. In no responsible quarter was effective action taken while the time for action was ripe. In default of such action the country drifted into financial disaster.
When the inevitable period of deflation and depression came, in their sheer extent financial losses, economic disorganization and panicky fear of complete political, social and financial collapse, turned out to be the most disastrous in the history of the country, and for generations are likely to leave their imprint upon our government and business organizations. The prosperity of industry had been prolonged by the artificial props of the instalment plan, foreign loans and stock market profits. When these failed, the demand for industrial products fell. Sharp price cuts at this time might have brought readjustment in conditions of supply and demand, and an early end to the depression. But restriction of industrial output, with artificial maintenance of high prices, only made matters worse. Rapidly declining pay-rolls, the inevitable result of a policy of restriction, brought a further decline in demand not only for industrial products but farm products, and intensified the decline in the price of farm products-a condition which soon thoroughly demoralized agriculture and almost completely destroyed1 the buying power of the farmers.
The ruin of the farmers reacted upon the demand for factory products, leading the restrictionists to resort to still further restrictions, and so on month after month in a vicious declining spiral of deflation; in industry, deflation primarily in output and payrolls, and only secondly in prices; in agriculture, deflation in prices but not in production.
Statistics of industrial production and prices point strongly to the conclusion that the years of depression in industry were characterized, not by competitive cutting of prices among the producers in a given industry as a means of stimulating demand and maintaining output, but by competitive restriction of output among the industries for the purpose of maintaining prices. It was this policy of adjusting supply to demand, a policy substituted for the old-fashioned one of adjusting price to demand, that prolonged, deepened and is helping to continue the depression. There were, of course, other important contributing causes such as the slaughter of prices on the stock and bond markets, the deflation of bank credit, the demoralization in foreign trade and the financial crises in foreign countries.
There is one most important point which it is essential should be clear to all, and
that is that neither the factor of declining bank credits nor of money in circulation forced the deflation of business. The major causes of the decline in business were, first, the maldistribution of buying power arising from the lack of balance between the prices of finished, manufactured goods and the prices of raw materials and wages, and second, the lack of desire of those with buying power in the form of cash or bank credit to use it. Instead of money being scarce in Canada at the present time, it is in fact very plentiful. It would seem an adequate reply to the claim that we are suffering from a money shortage to point out that all money rates have fallen substantially. Well might the minister say in his budget address, as reported at page 1215 of Hansard:
Monetary policy has a role to play during depressions. That role is an important one; although I am bound to say that as a medicine for depressions monetary techniques are far more effective when applied before rather than after the event.
It is in the light of the above evidence of plentiful money, and of the facts brought out in my analysis of the existing conditions, that I beg the government to do all in its power to prevent any possible recurrence of the 1929 financial misfortune. It is clearly evident that speculation is again finding its path into the country's stock market, that the gap between wages and prices is increasing and that signs of inflation are becoming more and more evident. If we wish to prevent an artificial boom followed by a devastating financial and commercial collapse, we must take steps while the time is still ripe to control the recovery of this country before it gets out of bounds.
The income of the farmer is again lagging behind the advance in the price of finished manufactured goods. This must be stopped if the farmers are not to be oppressed until they are living below the subsistence level. It is essential that a fair share of the increased national income should be distributed among the present unemployed and those living below the subsistence level. In fact, until all are at least on the subsistence level, for sound economic and just social reasons there should be no increase in the wages or profits of those who are at present living above that level. If this country is ever to experience any degree of real prosperity we must have a more equal distribution of the national income. Those who are at present without a decent standard of living must be provided with one. A policy of continued public expenditure of relief funds will not bring this about. Only real increased production, to-
The Budget-Mr. Fleming

gether with a more equal and just distribution, ;can possibly enable the people to live above the subsistence level.
I believe the ultimate and fundamental object of all honest political endeavour in any country should be the raising of the standard of life. Let us follow this policy with the same diligent effort that we put forth for the betterment of our owni individual lives. Increased international trade will help, in fact it is essential, but it is not enough. There must not be a recurrence of what happened in 1929. The draft agenda for the world economic conference contains the following:
International action, however indispensable, cannot restore a normal economic situation unless the proper internal measures have been taken. Each individual country must be prepared to take the necessary steps to achieve internal equilibrium.
In conclusion I would suggest that we go blithely on the road to the full promise of our -nationhood, with Liberal principles the light to guide our way, and the happiness of our people our abiding purpose. Let us gamer from the variety of races within our borders the best that they have to give. If our prosperity must be protected, let us do it with wisdom. Let us not be inoculated by Tory Imperialism or militarism, but if the pathway of our destiny leads through a virile pacifism, Set us not stumble, but with dignity, charity :and honesty march triumphantly forward, a peaceful nation building contentment. May the [DOT]tribute of our children be:	They wrought
better than they knew.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first congratulate the hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. Fleming) on his very able address. I wish also to congratulate the government upon having within their ranks a free trader who is prepared to support a protectionist budget. I trust the hon. member will pardon me for not following his remarks, for what I have to say this evening will be confined to the amendment. I hope that at some other time I may have the opportunity of speaking on the main motion.
The amendment deals with what I believe is recognized as being the most serious problem in Canada, that of unemployment and relief. I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) has admitted that this is the most serious problem with which the government has to deal. Let me quote the amendment:
This house regrets that the government has failed to take effective measures to deal with the problem of unemployment.
[Mr. Fleming.!
I wish to put emphasis on the word " effective." I admit that the government have taken some measures, but we must decide whether or not they are effective measures. Let us consider what those measures are. In his address the other day the minister recited several measures taken by the government since they came into office. The minister, first, spent some time discussing the relief camps which were set-up in this country at one time. I shall not go into the history of these camps as the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) covered it very thoroughly the other night. I shall not recall the conditions which existed at the time these camps came into being, other than to say that they were established to take care of the single unemployed men who were crowding into our cities, riding our trains and generally trekking throughout the country. They were never intended to be permanent, but during the time they were in existence they played an important part in relieving the problem of unemployment; they functioned as clearing houses, through which passed 31,502 men to useful employment. That achievement I think was worth while. As I say, it was never intended that these camps should continue, and upon the minister's instructions they were closed. A number of us coming from British Columbia recall as I do very clearly, the time they were closed. In my riding some 800 men were turned out on the road. They were men who had been faithful and had not been involved in any disturbance; they had worked well and were at home in those camps. They were turned out with their packs and drifted along the highways to the cities. The equipment from the different camps was gathered together, the shovels and other tools carefully oiled, sorted and packed into crates, the bedding washed and packed, and everything was stored in a central camp. The other day the minister told us, "To this time the camps have not been re-opened." I do not know how he can be ignorant of the fact that a number of them have been opened. The equipment, the property of the federal government, which was so carefully stored has been taken back to some of these camps and is now in use. In my riding there are about 300 men in the camps, and they are carrying on work similar to what they did before.
The minister mentioned the other day one measure, termed an arrangement with the railways. There were 9,224 men transferred from the camps to railway work, and according to information given by the department,

The Budget-Mr. Barber
7,773 men worked until the gangs were broken up; in other words, they completed six months' employment. The cost to the taxpayers of this country was over 32,600,000.
Another measure was the farm placement scheme. The minister tells us that throughout Canada 46,000 men were placed. My information, which is from Victoria and is I think authentic, is that 215 were placed in British Columbia.
Another measure was forestry work. We are told by the minister that 5,000 additional men have been employed, mainly in British Columbia, in forestry work. I think the minister must have included labour in the logging industry, which cannot be credited to any action on his part but to the empire trade agreements and, to some extent, the Canada-United States trade agreement. The latest information I have from Victoria is that 1,131 men are employed in forestry work in the province under the category of relief measures.
Another scheme was the home improvement plan. I believe it was unanimously supported in this house. It is good as far as it goes, but I doubt whether it will give much employment to men on relief. It seems to me that- a citizen who undertakes to repair his house, to put on a new verandah or redecorate the interior, is not likely to go down to the unemployment office or to relief headquarters to get a man; he wants the work well and properly done and he is going to get a mechanic to do it, someone he knows is a first-class workman. For that reason I do not think this measure will be a means of putting any considerable number of unemployed to work, and the expenditure of one and a half to two million dollars for this purpose is only a drop in the bucket.
These are some of the measures which the government has taken, directed to the solution of the problem of unemployment. Another measure, which I believe the minister considers most important is the setting up of the employment commission. Hon. members recall that, last session, the government induced parliament to pass an act setting up a commission to which the matter of unemployment was to be referred. Apparently it has gone the way of all bodies of this kind, in setting up an elaborate scheme. The commission consists of seven members. Of course they are not paid salaries. It would be an insult to offer salaries to persons who come forward and offer to serve their country. But a kindly government suggests that they should have a living allowance, and with the exception of the chairman they have accepted it. They are paid a living allowance of
twenty dollars a day, and in addition their travelling expenses. British Columbia was honoured in having the commission's lady member chosen from that province. It is interesting to note that she has drawn in living allowances and travelling expenses from May 15 to the end of January 35,590.93. Whatever other qualifications she may or may not possess, those of us who live in British Columbia know that she has one- she is a faithful follower of the Liberal party.
There is another commission member from the west who volunteered his services: a defeated Liberal candidate from Saskatchewan. He has drawn $4,559.05. The minister told, us the other day that the commissioners have been paid since May 15 in living allowances and travelling expenses $18,666. Its members are furnished with offices and telephone, secretaries and stenographers, all. of which goes to make up what he told us was cost of personnel: 316,888.
There is under the commission, the youth committee, which has cost $8,951. The members are not in receipt of salaries but are given a living allowance of fifteen dollars per day each. Going through the orders in council it was noticed that the chairman could not live on the fifteen dollars and was granted an additional five dollars. He happens to be a defeated Liberal candidate from British Columbia. There is also, a women's committee of five, each drawing fifteen dollars per day living allowance; the minister mentioned that the total cost to date was $2,916; they are studying the problem. Also a living allowance of $25 per day has been granted the director of public welfare for some temporary services. I do not understand why the government does not pay salaries, instead of insisting on calling these grants "living allowances." Nor is it clear why the amount of these allowances should vary, why it costs more for one person to live than another. That brings to mind a little article I saw in a Toronto paper the other day, contributed by a man named Oxford, He is referring to the grain inquiry, which is another creature of this government:
Mr. Justice Turgeon, commissioner for the gram inquiry, receives $35 a day as a living allowance. From inquiries made of some housewives around here, the opinion is that he should do fairly well on that, and get three good meals every day. It would even run to an egg-nog about 11 a.m. and still leave him with enough to buy a packet of cigarettes a day as a "living allowance" multiplied by five and a half -assuming that he knocks off when the whistle blows on Saturday-ought to get him in as the star boarder in any town, with a cup of tea brought up in the morning. . . .
The Budget-Mr. Barber

Just to show how discriminating and careful our judicial officers are when spending our money, they have it figured out that Hon. J. L. Ralston, K.C., counsel for the grain inquiry, is only worth $20 a day for his hay and oats. Seems a shame to scale him down $15 a day, but perhaps he's on a diet, or maybe he can't eat as much as Mr. Justice Turgeon. Quite obviously he can only have one egg for breakfast, and he gets no dessert for dinner. A man can't have everything on just $110 a week. You know yourself how far that goes when you are dragging the basket around on Saturday night and the wife is picking up three tins of soup for a quarter.
Of course, Mr. Ralston is being paid $200 a day for his services, with no lost time for rainy weather and no early closing on Wednesday. On the other hand, he doesn't get paid for overtime-just a straight $200 a day-take it or leave it, but you -wouldn't expect any part of that to go for the feed bill. Certainly not. Twenty dollars a day is what^ the government figure his pork and beans will cost, and he should keep within that limit, even if he has to do without tea and toast in the afternoon.
Speaking of cuts, here is the unkindest cut of all. J. E. Coyne, barrister, only gets a miserable $10 a day living expenses. How does he get by? Apparently he can only eat half as much as the Hon. Mr. Ralston. You can readily imagine Mr. Coyne walking round the block at lunch time, munching a bag of peanuts, and thinking of what a fine fish and chip supper he will have. What is worse and more of it, he only gets $50 a day for the job, and it may not last more than a few months.
The really bright spot in the line-up of the grain commission is that the secretary is not listed for any additional salary or living allowance. Presumably he is expected to stay with friends, or drop in on acquaintances at meal times and send -his washing home collect.
This government continues to spend money quite freely in providing "living allowances"- I am sure there are many people throughout Canada including the wives of farmers who would like a guaranteed living allowance of, say. 820.00 or $25.00 per month.
There is another organization, under the employment commission which was set up by the orders in council cited by my leader, and the Minister -of Labour (Mr. Rogers) told us the other night that this organization, a sort of duplication of the bureau of statistics, has cost over $40,000.

speechtext:
And according to the supplementary estimates it will cost $125,000 next year. That is plain. The minister charged my leader with creating an impression contrary to the facts when he recited the order in council. He said that some of these em-

ployees were seconded and others were temporary employees; nevertheless, if you go through the order in council, you will find that they were authorized fior employment in this organization, and the funds provided for the organization next year will pay for their services. As regards this organization set up under the commission the minister said -1 believe he interrupted the leader of the opposition when he made the statement-"that it is concerned with registration as provided in the statute." I was of the opinion that the registration had been completed, and my authority for that is a clause that appears in the speech from the throne, on January 14, 1937, at page 3 of Hansard:
A registration of unemployed persons on relief has been completed.
I do not understand, therefore, why this organization is to be continued if registration is completed. However, it is to be continued, because provision is made in the estimates for the purpose. The whole organization is an elaborate and most costly scheme. The supplementary estimates brought down a few days ago contain an item for the National Employment Commission of $150,000; an item for the National Employment Commission, registration, $125,000; and an item for the unemployment relief branch, $200,000; and the heading under which these items are enumerated indicates that they are for administration purposes, salaries, living allowances and travelling expenses. So that if this appropriation is for the maintenance of the organization it would seem that more orders in council yvill be passed providing for a larger staff. Let me summarize these measures that have been taken by the government.
First, railway work. The minister informs us that 9,224 men were taken from the relief camps and put to work; 46,000 under farm placement measure,-215 being in British Columbia; 5,000 in connection with forestry work, the statistics showing that 1,131 are engaged in this work in British Columbia.
As regards the home improvement plan, $1,500,000 or $2,000,000 has already been spent on this project, and that should give some employment. Then there is the other organization to which I have already referred. These are the measures that the government has undertaken, and as far as I can see they are not what I would call effective measures.
And what about the results in meeting this problem? Sometimes we can judge best by results. A good many figures were placed on Hansard the other day and I shall not repeat them all.	The number of unemployed in Canada in February 1935 was 552,000; October 1935, 435,000; in Janu-

ary 1936, it was 556,000, and in December
1936,	502,000. In January 1937, the number was 500,000. In other words, we still have
500,000	unemployed throughout Canada, and if you will sum up all that the government has done in its various measures to cope with this great problem you will find that they will hardly make a dint in it. Then we have the number of those on relief. In February 1934 it was 1,491,059, and in February 1935, 1,433,891. In September 1936, it was 1,029,156, and in January 1937, 1,301,530.
