subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance in his usual able manner has drawn to our attention the increase in trade and pointed out the great increase in production, but surely there is something wrong. If trade and productions are increasing, more work must be in progress, yet the demand for public relief is not falling. Let me suggest to the minister and to the government that they direct their attention to the reduction in the burden of taxation in this country. The increased burden from year to year is doing more to prevent recovery than any other factor that I know of. Some hon. gentleman may say that the rate of taxation has not been increased. Well, the rate does not cut so much figure; it is the burden of taxation that counts. If you go over the speech of the minister in regard to taxation you find that that burden is increasing, it has increased this year over last, and the estimate for next year shows an increase over this.
First I should like to deal with customs tax. In years eone by we were reminded over
and over again that this is a tax, and told how unfair the tax was. That came from the low tariff people and some of the free traders who are associated with the Liberal party. Let us look at the customs tax. In the year 1933-34 the amount taken from the people by customs tax was 866,395,000. This year, 1936-37, it is put at 881,500,000, and the Minister of Finance says that next year he is going to take from the people of this country by way of customs tax 890,000,000-an increase from $66,000,000 to 890,000,000 in five years.
Someone may say:	That affects only certain people. Before I left British 'Columbia a farmer came to me with a document which shows that he had bought some beet pulp, a by-product of the sugar factory at Bellingham, Washington, a few miles from my district. This load of beet pulp cost him $18. When he came to the border they listed it as 3,000 pounds of beet pulp and molasses, cattle food with molasses, the value of the sacks was included in the price-it was packed in new sacks-and they fixed the valuation at 846.73. To make it even they called it $47, and the duty charged was 20 per cent. The duty amounted to $9.40; excise tax $1.69; brokerage $1.50; total charge $12.59 on $18 worth of stuff. That did not take place under a high tariff Tory government; that took place on November 23 last year. Yet the minister says he is going to take more and more from the people of Canada next year; he is going to increase the customs tax burden to $90,000,000.
Then the sales tax. In 1933-34 the burden of this tax amounted to $61,392,000; this year it is $115,500,000, and the estimate for next year is $131,000,000. The people of Canada, ten and a half millions, must dig up next year for the Minister of Finance some $15,000,000 more than this year in the way of sales tax- and everyone pays the sales tax.
The income tax rose from $61,399,000 in 1933-34 to an estimated $113,000,000 for 193738, which is about $10,000,000 more than the present year. Still the minister says the rate has not been raised. I am not here to defend the coupon clipper or the big moneyed men; they of course have their troubles. But the ordinary taxpayer, the men who pay income tax in the lower categories have a hard time. We have the income tax imposed by this government, the provincial income tax, municipal taxes, and all kinds of taxes. As a result a man to-day is so hampered by taxation that he is not in a position to expand his business or give increased employment.
The excise tax this year is $45,500,000, and the minister says that next year he must raise $47,500,000. the burden of this increase in
The Budget-Mr. Barber

excise taxes increased by $2,000,000 in one year. That 3 per cent excise tax which hon. gentlemen opposite when in opposition said was only an extra customs tariff still remains.
Then we have stamp and special taxes. In 1935-36 the burden of taxation under this item was $35,181,000; this year it is $38,100,000, and the minister says that for next year he is going to increase that burden to $42,000,000. This includes the sugar tax, and, oh, what we did hear in years gone by about the sugar tax! I could quote hon. members who were then on this side of the house; pages of Hansard could be filled with quotations from speeches made by them at that time condemning this tax. I recall one by the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacLean), and I quote him because he is about the furthest east. On May 11, 1934, after profesting vigorously against this tax, he said, as reported in Hansard at page 2997:
I am glad the government reduced the tax by one per cent, but in the circumstances I think the tax should have been entirely wiped out. There are other ways of raising revenue without resorting to the taxation of articles of food which are necessities of life.
This government has been in power for almost a year and a half; this is their second nession, and still the sugar tax remains.
Now let us see about the total taxes. The total to be collected for the year 1937-38 is estimated at $425,500,000. That is the burden of taxation on the Canadian people; about $8,000,000 a week, close to $4 for every man, woman and child in Canada. That figure is an increase of $41,000,000 over the present year, and an increase of $121,000,000 over 1934-35. How can ten and a half million people continue to bear this burden? Taxation is strangling industry to-day; it is the bugbear of the Canadian people and the main factor in preventing the return of prosperity to this country.
In view of the measures put forth by the government for the solution of this great problem of unemployment in this country I am prepared to support the amendment.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to draw the attention of the government to the just claims of my constituents of Laval-Two Mountains in connection with a matter of national importance which I have not ceased to agitate in this house ever since I became a member of parliament. The matter is that of the produce of market-gardens, the value of which, for the province of Quebec alone, reached $5,442,000 in 1935 and $6,221,000 in 1936. I note with satisfaction that, owing to the seasonal tariff, the

market-gardeners obtained for their produce last year much more remunerative prices than formerly. In fact, notwithstanding a lower production, the value of their products in 1936 exceeded that of 1935 by nearly $800,000 in Quebec province alone. I have therefore requested and shall again request the government to apply at the proper time this seasonal tariff which has been so beneficial to the producers. I may add that the statistics which I have just quoted have been graciously supplied to me by the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), to whom I offer my thanks.
Field crops, cattle-raising and dairying are sources of wealth on which depends the prosperity of the country. By means of substantial grants, generous help and constant support, our governments owe it to themselves to develop these immense resources in the best interests of Canada. The present government had done a great deal for agriculture. It has negotiated with other countries trade agreements that have greatly benefited the farming community. Let us not stop there. Let us seek to popularize agricultural science. Our ideal should be the full development of the fertility with which providence has endowed our land.
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the workmen of my constituency, I ask the government to proceed with certain undertakings of public interest. I have several times drawn the attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) and of the management of the Canadian National Railways to the necessity of completing the construction of the Canadian National line from Calumet Point to Oka. The residents of the village of Oka have too long been isolated from the surrounding towns and parishes, particularly from Montreal, during the winter months. The beautiful country surrounding Oka and the lake of Two Mountains is one of the finest tourist resorts in my province. It is frequented each summer by many thousands of visitors. By adding about four miles to its line the Canadian National Railways will surely find there some of the revenue they so badly need.
Having referred to the interesting question of tourist travel, I should not pass over in silence the failure to build the projected section of the trans

Canada highway in my constituency. The necessity of this portion of the highway has been recognized. Plans and specifications for it were drawn a long time ago by engineers of the former Quebec government, in the district of Saint-Martin, Sainte-Dorothee and Saint-Eustache. Why was the execution of the work deferred or given up? I do not know. However, the

The Budget-Mr. Lacombe
building of that road would have resulted immediately in giving employment to hundreds of unemployed. That is why I insist upon the construction of that part of the trans-Canada highway in the constituency of Laval-Two Mountains, from the limits of St. Martin to Lachute. Tourists travelling on that road will wonder at the beautiful scenery, as well as the extent of the admirable work carried on by our truck gardeners and farmers, and the example to be drawn from it. Where-ever you cast your eyes in that peerless farming country you will see vast tracts of green vegetation, abounding crops, and dainty houses, a symbol of comfort acquired through perseverance and work.
May I also Call upon the government to dredge the Back river channel from the St. Vincent de Paul dam to lake of Two Mountains. These works are essential in the interest of the tourist trade which so largely adds to the prosperity of the country as a whole. There are other things that I shall ask for when we take up the public works estimates, for they are more of a local character.
Before I resume my seat, I cannot but speak of the want of confidence motion of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). It would be sufficient to emphasize the absurdity of this motion. The mover is the former head of the government; he charges the present administration with having failed in its duty by following a policy which cannot efficiently solve the unemployment problem. I deny the former prime minister the right to censure the commendable efforts of the present government in that direction. It has been in power barely fifteen months and already the number of people on relief has substantially decreased. At any rate, are those who are at present administering this country responsible for the baneful and ruinous policy of direct relief? It is no other than the present leader of the opposition who gave birth to this octopus? Did he not summon a special session of parliament for that very purpose? However, if I remember aright, his government was to end unemployment in a rather short time. Let us be fair. Since the beneficent results of its policy of economic recovery are already being felt let us at least pay the present government the tribute that it deserves. For my part, considering the commendable efforts of the present administration, I deem it my duty to oppose the motion of want of confidence of the right hon. leader of the opposition. I shall go further in asserting that many farmers in my constituency have more than once expressed their satisfaction at the betterment of the prices of farm products.
Nobody can deny that there is now greater activity in trade and business, more confidence and hope among our people.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot end these remarks without drawing the attention of the house and the government to the administration of the Canadian Farm Loan Act. There are unaccountable delays in the administration of this measure. According to representations that were made to me, the examination of the titles of farmers applying for a loan ought to be done much more rapidly. This examination, especially in the province of Quebec, sometimes becomes a complete maze. The attending notary and the officers of the commission cannot find their way out of it. The farmer frequently loses thereby not only his time but also his borrowing power. In my humble opinion, it is imperative that some one should be appointed as a go-between in each electoral division or court district. Such a man would have to be quite industrious. His work would consist in securing, with the least possible delay, all the necessary papers for the transaction. Some might object, on the ground that these appointments would involve a considerable cost. Let me answer at once that, taking into consideration the necessary efficiency of the act., this cost would be a mere trifle.
Now, what about the famous creditors and farmers arrangement act? During the last session I requested the repeal of this act, which is so greatly unfair to the farmer and the creditor. The privy council has just decided that this act is constitutional. It is no doubt a mere counterpart of the Bankruptcy act. The former government has no reason to be proud of having given birth to such a monster of injustice. Mr. Speaker, before that act destroys all self-reliance among our people, would it not be possible to replace it by a more elastic, broader and more expeditious farm loan act? If a day ever comes when the arrangement act is replaced by a farm loan act adapted to the needs of destitute farmers who would give the authorities the guarantee of their steadfastness and their work, besides the guarantee of their equipment and buildings, on that day we will have achieved much for the rehabilitation of agriculture in Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret I was unable to follow the previous speaker (Mr. Lacombe) in French, but I am sure his speech must have been good judging by the applause he received on taking his seat.
I hope I shall not be accused, as have some other hon. members, of speaking politi-
The Budget-Mr. Fair

cally. I have no political axe to grind, and for that reason I intend to speak as a practical farmer from the west. I say "practical" because I notice that quite a number who are listed as farmers turn out to be gentlemen farmers, who raise nothing but their hats.
One part of the budget pleased me particularly, and that was the government's compliance with the representations of a year ago for pensions for the blind. I am glad the government has seen fit to grant the pension, and I trust that in the near future the qualifying age for the blind may be placed far below forty, because hon. members in all sections of the house must realize that it keeps those of us with good eyesight busy to make a living, and for that reason we ought to remember the peculiar difficulties of those men and women who have not the blessing of eyesight.
My interest in the budget is particularly in matters relating to agriculture, as well as some other matters to which reference has been made. However, as other hon. members are better qualified to deal with some of the subjects brought out in the speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), I shall confine my observations mainly to agriculture. May I say at the outset that it is our primary industry. Speaking of agriculture, the minister said:
Agricultural production suffered in 1936 through unfavourable weather during the growing season. Improved prices, however, resulted in a money return for field crops greater than in any year since 1930, and amounted to approximately $600,000,000, an increase of about 17 per cent over 1935.
With regard to wheat, the 1936 yield was about 52-7 million bushels below that of 1935, and was the smallest crop since 1919. Drought conditions again played havoc in certain areas, destroying crops completely in some districts and reducing to meagre levels the yield in others. In spite of the smaller 1936 yield, however, the value of this crop was substantially above the value of the 1935 crop, due to greatly enhanced prices, which are again reaching levels which promise more profitable and stable conditions foT the western farmer.
While prices are better than they were, the wheat crop last year averaged only about eight bushels per acre, which I believe is about only half the usual average of the Canadian crop. It would seem therefore that for anything like a decent living the price we received for our grain last fall was not nearly sufficient-and when I say not nearly sufficient I mean that very thing.
Listening to the arguments in the house, if one did not know better he might be led to believe that the action of the government in putting the wheat board out of business was justifiable. As one who has suffered
I Mr. Fftir.l
from that action, may I say that I do not agree with it. Going back more than thirty years, farmers in western Canada were producing large quantities of grain, and just as they are to-day were being deprived of much of the profits justly belonging to them. A man named Partridge, of Sintaluta, in company with some others began to take steps to improve conditions, and made a considerable amount of progress. I believe the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) will remember those good old days. May I say I am sorry he has seen fit to take part in getting rid of the wheat board. I suggest that as a western man he should have known what western farmers are up against and should have done his share to keep the board in operation.
More than thirty years ago the farmers in the west began to fight their own battles. They did not do so because they wanted an excuse for fighting, but because they were not receiving their just rights, and they decided that the fellows under their own hats were their best friends. The Canada Grain Act was not then so much in the producers' favour as it is to-day, and we found some years ago that its provisions were not being observed. People were not getting the grading to which they were entitled; they were being short weighted, were being deprived of their turn in getting cars for loading, and several other things. I can remember occasions more than twenty years ago when taking loads of No. 1 wheat a distance of more than thirty miles I was told upon reaching the elevator just about dark by the gentleman who came alongside that he was very sorry but they had no more room for No. 1, but that they had room for No. 3, and he ended up by saying, "If you want to take that, all right; I can unload it." That trick was played time after time, but at last the farmers, who are not quite as easy as they are thought to be, woke up to the fact that they were being gypped. They did a little work and finally got some relief. The united grain growers and other provincial organizations got started, and then the war came along. In 1917 wheat prices were rising along with prices of other commodities. The war had been in full swing for some time but the farmers were not allowed to profiteer. On June 11, 1917, a wheat board was created and the price of wheat was set at $2.40 per bushel.
When the war was over and there seemed a chance that the price of wheat would come down, the government of that day decided that the board was no longer necessary. But the farmers, feeling that the board had been organized to keep prices from going up,

The Budget-Mr. Fair
thought that it might as well work the other way. In July, 1919, the Canadian wheat board was formed, and an initial price of $2.15 per bushel was set. Those who delivered wheat to the board were given participation certificates, which many farmers sold for a few cents, or even gave away. However, under the good management of the board an interim payment of 30 cents per bushel and a final payment of 18 cents a bushel was made, making the total price for the crop of that year $2.63 per bushel. That board went out of existence on August 16, 1920.
I can remember hauling a carload of wheat a distance of thirty miles that year. When I shipped it out of the elevator I took an advance payment of $1 per bushel. Shortly afterwards the price rose to $2.06 per bushel, but this was before my wheat had1 got to Winnipeg. There was some delay in my car getting through so I was not able to sell. The price then dropped to $1.56 per bushel, but I was eventually able to sell at $1.83 per bushel. If there had been a wheat board in existence I believe I would have been saved a lot of worry. I had not been in business very long at that time and I had lots of debts to pay, but I was willing to pay them. As the board was not operating, I had to take what I could get on the open market.
In the years preceding 1922 the wheat producers had been working hard to get a national wheat board. The agitation had grown so strong by 1922 that the dominion government decided to pass the necessary legislation. However, it was first necessary to have enabling legislation passed by the provinces. The necessary legislation was passed by Saskatchewan and Alberta, but Manitoba would not agree. I do not know whether that was because the grain exchange was located in that province and there were too many advocates preaching in its favour, but the result was that no wheat board was formed.
In 1923 the Alberta farmers led the way in forming a voluntary wheat pool. In 1924 Saskatchewan and Manitoba linked up. At first the provinces sold as separate organizations, but a short time afterwards they united and sold as one organization. This worked out very nicely until the crash of 1929. Some say that agriculture was the cause, but those of us who have looked around and studied things a little do not agree with that statement. Late in 1929 the price of wheat slumped badly, and the wheat pools got into difficulties. The federal government had to come to their assistance a little later on. In 1930 the price of wheat dropped to a very low level, and the result was that the wheels of industry began to slow up.
The government then decided that something would have to be done, and the result was the formation of a stabilization board by the then Conservative government. After this board was formed the Stamp commission was appointed to endeavour to find out what was the trouble. This commission pointed out in its report that speculators were necessary to the successful operation of the grain exchange. As there were no speculators at that time, the operations of the grain exchange were limited. The crash of 1929 had ruined a number of these speculators while others had learned their lesson and were out of the game for the time being.
At this time the western pools and other farmer organizations were pressing hard for the formation of a wheat board, but they were unable to get it. The government continued the stabilization operations under the chairmanship of Mr. McFarland. However, in 1935, the wheat board legislation was finally enacted. This board was headed by Mr. McFarland, and it started out to operate with a fixed price of 87i cents per bushel. When the price was first set it looked rather low to the western pool representatives who wanted a price set of 95 cents per bushel; the grain exchange representatives wanted the price set a little above 70 cents per bushel, and the result was a compromise at the 87-J-cent level.
If the wheat had been sold as it should have been, I believe everything would have been all right. Under the terms of the legislation, farmers who delivered grain were given participation certificates which entitled them to share in any profits which might be made later on. I remember holding some of these certificates for some time-in fact, I believe I have some yet-but it was finally realized that there would be nothing else coming in, that there was quite a loss on the operations. When I look back and remember the fight put up by the Liberal party when in opposition to that legislation, I was surprised to learn that the wheat board had turned back $8,000,000 of the money that had been advanced. As some of the farmers in the west said, they did very well in spite of themselves.
After the Liberal government came into power a change in the wheat policy was made, and also a change of wheat board. Some say a fire sale took place; perhaps that is right; perhaps not. However, Mr. Murray, the head of the present wheat board, giving evidence before the parliamentary committee last year, had this to say:
I mentioned yesterday in the opening statement which I read that we considered one of our principal duties was to dispose of the burdensome part of the surplus.
The Budget-Mr. Fair

Now, the price did not seem to have anything to do with that. The job was to get rid of the wheat, and when it comes to getting rid of the wheat we have to agree that the board made an excellent job of it. A little further on Mr. Murray said:
I think I used the phrase that it hung like a millstone around the necks of our farmers since 1928. _ I might mention that that is not my description. If I may be permitted I will say that that is the description given to that surplus by Mr. John I. McFarland on December 8, 1934, if my memory is correct.
Now, we could not afford to wait for one, two, three or four weeks or to wait until it was found out what the policy of the board was going to be. At least we did not think we could. We wanted to get some action. We called meetings of the exporters and millers. They are the only salesmen of Canadian wheat. The act tells us specifically that "ii ,^ave Sot to use them. It means to use all branches of the trade without discrimination. So we called meetings and we told them the_ new board was there; that we wanted their cooperation and we wanted them to get busy and sell all the wheat and flour for export that they could possibly sell. We asked for suggestions as to what we might do to help them accomplish that. We told them we did not expect them to do business for nothing.
We agree with that; we have no quarrel whatever with the view that they should be paid for their services. But there is one circumstance there which seems strange. The farmers grew the wheat, and the grain exchange were asked for suggestions how to sell it. I do not know whether that strikes anyone else as odd, but it does me, because such transactions are quite expensive. Again:
One of the suggestions they made to us was that we agree to sell them their hedges against export sales made between the close of the market one day and the opening of the market the next day at not more than one-quarter of a cent over the previous day's close.
That thereby a long step was made in the selling out of the farmers' interests cannot, I believe, be successfully contradicted. Mr. Murray further says:
We made that agreement with them, or gave them an undertaking, whichever you like to call it, with one proviso. We explained to them that we were not handling our own money and our own funds.
At that committee meeting I asked Mr. Murray:
Is that the first time that protection of that kind was extended to exporters?
The answer was:
t No, sir, but it is the first time it was done right out in the open.
A little further on he says:
We, wanting them to have that wheat freely, gave them that assurance. We did not anticipate it would continue for an indefinite time. 
We wanted to get them started. It was discontinued on December 20, for this reason; the market in the pit itself was being killed.
If one analyzes that statement a little something worth while may be gained. Mr. Murray goes on:
People having done an export business, instead of coming into the pit in the morning to buy their wheat, would come direct to us. It was an easier way to do it.
I contend that it was also a cheaper way. This, however, is what has happened; we find that very good progress is indicated by showing a deficit in wheat board operations. I believe a great effort was made to destroy the wheat board and its usefulness. Instead of leaving the man there who had been doing good work, work which so far as I know was satisfactory to the west, the government put in a new man who has fought the wheat board, wheat pools, and farmers' organizations as long as I can remember.

I know he was an inventor. I also know some other things that happened a little later on. While this committee was sitting, Mr. Murray gave out a statement. I do not know whether it was prepared by himself or by the board, but it was probably composed before he left Winnipeg. This is what he said:	,
Until recent years our surplus wheat was absorbed into world trade and no one knew, except in the most general way, just how or where it went. The little consideration we gave to this question ten years ago is not sufficient now.
World wheat trade which averaged 721,309,000 bushels for the ten years 1920 to 1929 was large enough to absorb the surplus from average crops in exporting countries.
This situation no longer exists, and if wheat is to retain the position it has occupied in the production of our national wealth, we must wake up to the importance of the problem. T might interject and say that from 1926 to 1930 inclusive, the value of wheat exported was 32 per cent of the total Canadian exports. From 1931 to 1935 inclusive, it was 25 per cent: that is, wheat and flour.
World trade in wheat last year, including
26,000,000 bushels imported by the United States, was only 520 million bushels. This year, including perhaps 50 million bushels which may be imported by the United States, it wiil probably not be more than 520 million bushels. Excluding the United States this means an average for the two years of less than 500 million bushels of wheat taken by importing countries.
We cannot count on the United States continuing as an importer and they may in a few months again become exporters. Europe may not be as successful as in recent years in growing large crops, but no sensible person

The Budget-Mr. Fair
would advocate in dealing with this problem that our main dependence should be on Providence continuing to help us through crop failures in other countries.
Then Mr. Murray comes to a very sensible part of his statement. He says:
Our problem for the future then is, briefly: normal crops on present acreage in exporting countries will give from 640 to 740 million bushels exportable surplus. The available market may be only 500 to 550 million bushels.
How can Canada continue to grow crops of 375 to 425 million bushels and fit into this picture without again piling up unwieldy and burdensome surpluses.
_ Can we. as a nation, tackle this problem intelligently? If we continue as we have for the past few years we will not do so.
I agree with that, and I believe that the only way to handle it is through a system of orderly marketing, which can be done only with a national board handling all the crop.
If I might refer for a moment to any of the years gone by, I might take at random 1925, just to show how the wheat goes on the market from our western farms. In September of 1925, 86,546,000 bushels was marketed; in October, 58,888,000; November, 85,134,000; December, 51,594,000; January, 24,074,000; February, 14,394,000; March, 10,215,000; April, 5,741.000; May, 3,580,000; June, 6,458,000; July, 4,200,000; August, 4,396,000. If hon. members will study these figures they will realize that in the first month the new crop was moving, 86,000,000 bushels were marketed, while in August of the next year only 4,396,000 bushels were marketed. From our experience of a number of years we know that as soon as all that wheat goes on the market, with nothing but an open market to trade on, the price immediately drops; and the wheat has to go on the market because, as I think is well known, the western farmers for a number of years have been in a pretty tough spot.
With all this wheat going on the market, and with depressed prices, somebody buys the hedges, and you will find that the price of wheat drops considerably and goes up again when the light marketings commence. That means that the farmer sells his wheat at a low price, and the speculator, who is allowed to operate uncontrolled, makes a profit out of the wheat. A very good example of that was given this fall when a large proportion of the wheat, seventy per cent of it, was sold at an average of 80 cents a bushel, and then we find that in the months that followed it was around the $1.30 mark. It is obvious that if the wheat board had been in existence there would not have been so many calls for help from the west. The west had been discriminated against in this and many other ways.

I understand that it is likely there will be another rise in farm machinery prices, although I was told not long ago that one of the big machine companies in the past ten years had paid an average of 6-3 per cent to its shareholders. That is not so bad. I believe I also saw the statement that some $29,000,000 of profits had been reported for one of these machinery companies. There is also a suggestion that a large secret reserve of something like $40,000,000 exists in one of these companies. We do not find very much relief at the other end, however.
In case anyone from the west has any kick on this, I will read from the Saskatchewan Liberal of February 18, 1937, part of an address by the hon. T. C. Davis, K.C., Attorney General. This is from a radio address he delivered on February 9:
In our development, as I have said, we sought capital and secured it. Money was loaned and borrowed on the basis of our agricultural product ion. We all assumed the conditions prevailing at the time the money was borrowed would continue to prevail without much change throughout the period of repayment.
All went comparatively well until the depression hit us in 1929. With the crash in the
The Budget-Mr. Fair

fall of that year the world was engulfed in an economic catastrophe, the severity of which has never been equalled in the history of the world. Prices tumbled, markets ceased to exist and the world seemed headed for chaos. Wheat prices went lower than they had ever been in the last 400 years. This catastrophe alone would have been sufficient to shake this province from stem to stern, cutting as it did at the very fundamentals of our economic life, but this was not all. Hand-in-hand with this catastrophe walked, for seven years, every plague and disaster known to agriculture. We nave had drought, dust storms, grasshoppers, rust and every conceivable disaster and pest.
For seven consecutive years we have gone through this, year after year, with fifty thousand farm families utterly destitute and having to be fed and clothed. Over a hundred million dollars had to be found to maintain human life-enough money, if so used, to pave every road in Saskatchewan.
The results of the combination of depression and drought is told in the production figures of agriculture over the last ten years. Listen to these figures:

The decrease in the cash income of the farmers of this province from, roughly, $275,000,000 a year in 1927 and 1928 down to $70,000,000 in 1931, 1932, 1933 and 1934, is a vital factor, evidencing the terrific strain upon the economic life of this province. There was a loss in cash revenue in those four years of over $800,000,000. The farmers' income has started to go up since 1933, but last year only reached $112,000,000, which is not nearly one-half of the amount realized in 1927 and 1928 when the majority of the debts were incurred.
Now if I were a good politician I should perhaps make good use of this. As I am not, I merely want to state that the average price of wheat from 1924 to 1929 inclusive was $1.43i. In a survey of a number of Saskatchewan farm incomes, we find that the income in 1925 averaged $2,856 per farm. In 1931 it dropped to $493, and in 1935 it had come back to $708, or approximately 25 per cent of what it was in 1925. The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Hyndman) a few days ago told us he was

sick and tired of hearing about wheat, and he went home and looked in the dictionary to find there were oats, 'barley and other crops. In that connection I can only say that:
A little learning is a dangerous thing;
Drink deep, or taste not the Pierian spring.
I remember those lines from the day I went to school, and I think they may be aptly applied to the hon. member and his remarks about agriculture.
Some hon. members from Quebec and Ontario, and others also, cannot imagine why we come here and kick about the treatment we are receiving. We are told that we must sell our wheat on the world market and take the world price for it. But we are buying machinery and other supplies in a protected market. Dealing in that protected market we find that in 1931 the net loss to Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta on account of tariffs amounted to $54,925,352. The gain for Ontario in that year alone amounted to $51,989,761 and to Quebec $31,685,885. This means that we lost $54,925,352, and Ontario alone had a net gain of $51,989,761.

Mr. JEAN-FRANQOiIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): The amendment we are discussing now is an invitation to speak about unemployment at large. In September, 1930, according to some information which has often been quoted, the total number of unemployed, including unemployables, was 117,930, or 1

The Budget-Mr. Pouliot
per cent of the population of this country. Before the last general election I asked the former Superintendent General of Indian Affairs of the previous government what was the number of Indians who had been receiving relief for the four or five previous years. He told me at first that it would take some time to gather that information; later I received another letter from him to the effect that it would involve considerable time and work in each agency, and some days later he told me he would endeavour to get the information requested; and finally, I never got it from him. But I got it this year from the present Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar). He stated on February 1, at page 419 of Hansard, that in 1930-31 there were 6,937 Indians on relief, with 9,088 dependents. I am sure that those Indians on relief and their dependents were included in the number of 117,930 unemployed quoted by the leader of the Tory party in 1930. The hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens), who was then Minister of Trade and Commerce, is quoted in the Canada Year Book for 1931, published by authority of his department, as follows respecting unemployment:
In Canada, as in other parts of the world, there was a general slackening in industrial activity during 1930, resulting in a lower level of employment than in 1929, and also than in some months of 1928. With these exceptions, however, the general index was higher than in previous years of the record.
Such was the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce of the previous government. There was less unemployment in 1930 than in the years before.
In September, 1930, the leader of the Tory party, fresh from the general election, overestimated the number of unemployed, but after he had been a few months in office the report of the Department of Labour of March, 1931, underestimated the number. To use his own words, when the present Prime Minister spoke of 117,000 unemployed in this country in September, 1930,
The right hon. gentleman (Mr. Mackenzie King) was doing this country an injury and a wrong, for there was no warrant for any such figure unless you included every babe in arms and every child from babyhood to the age of sixteen or seventeen as being among the unemployed.
The number 117,000 of unemployed, he then mentioned, included both unemployables and their dependents; so much so that on February 18, 1935, speaking on the unemployment insurance bill, he quoted figures which were a vindication of the policy followed by the Liberal government during the previous nine years. Why was that so? Because the figures he read showed only a small number
of unemployed under Liberal government, or about 1 per cent of the total population, and when the leader of the Tory party left office there were eleven times more.
There are three different classes of unemployed. First, there are those on relief; we know their number because we know the amount of money that is being paid to them. Second, there are those who work part time; as yet their number is unknown, and their case is very sad, Their incomes have been reduced very considerably. Many of them are too proud to accept relief. Others face this dilemma: either their meagre pay is deducted from their relief or their names are struck off the relief lists. Third, there are those who are supported by their own families, about whom we have no information as yet. At the last election the names of two hundred thousand young men were added to the lists, and we have no information as to how many of that number are unemployed.
In order to give an idea of what happened during the five years the previous government was in office, I desire to quote some extracts from the speeches from the throne and the prorogation speeches each year. They are on record as an expression of satisfaction put into the mouth of his excellency by the previous government. First I quote from the speech from the throne at the opening of the special session of 1930:
The necessity for dealing with exceptional economic conditions with the resultant unemployment has induced me to summon you at an earlier date than would otherwise be necessary. Measures will be submitted for your consideration, including amendments to the Customs Act and the customs tariff which it is anticipated will do much to meet the unusual conditions which now prevail.
Then, after 152 tariff items had been blindly increased and eleven items had been decreased, in order to meet the unusual conditions which then prevailed, we heard the prorogation speech, reading in part as follows:
I thank you for the prompt consideration which you have given to the measures submitted to you. and which are deemed necessary for the relief of unemployment in the dominion. It is my fervent hope and confident belief that these measures will prove effective in accomplishing the purposes for which they have been enacted.
Those were good wishes. Now I quote from the speech from the throne delivered at the opening of parliament in 1931:
I welcome you to your duties at a time when the nations of the world are passing through a period of great economic depression. Canada has not escaped it. But the Canadian people have met the trials of the moment with patience _ and fortitude, and are facing the future with the courage and faith which must
The Budget-Mr. Pouliot

triumph over every adversity... The problems which stand between us and ultimate prosperity are manifold and great. To be effectually met, they must first be understood. Confusion between cause and effect will but delay their solution.
During that, year the number receiving direct relief was 741,000, or about seven times as great as the number mentioned! by the leader of the Tory party in 1930. The disbursements made by the dominion under the relief act of 1931 were $42,740,000, or three times the disbursements under the relief act from September, 1930, to March, 1931. The prorogation speech of 1931 included this passage :
Since you entered upon the duties of the session, the world wide depression in economic conditions has grown more acute, and the consequent state of unemployment and distress in many parts of the country has been intensified through the partial failure of the wheat crop of western Canada. To augment existing relief measures, the governor in council has been empowered to take the necessary action to provide the maximum of employment and to aid, by such means as may be deemed expedient, the recovery from the adverse conditions arising primarily from the crop failure.
The great powers of fiurope and America, following the generous and constructive action of the president of the United States of America, which Canada wholeheartedly endorses, are unitedly striving for the re-establishment of better world conditions.
Better start at home!
Towards this purpose we may now effectively contribute, by steadfastly bending ourselves to the task of freeing Canada from the consequences of this universal state of economic depression and of the particular misfortune which has befallen the west; so that this country may be ready to take its place in the forefront of the world's recovery.
The speech from the throne for 1932 at the opening of the session was delivered on February 4 of that year, and from it I quote the following:
You enter upon your duties at a time of continuing and universal economic disturbance and distress. World conditions are beyond the control of the Canadian people. But I rejoice that their resolute adherence to policies designed for the welfare of the nation has minimized the adverse influence of external economic forces... The provisions made at the last session of parliament for unemployment and farm relief are proving effective.
You are successfully meeting difficult domestic problems. Conditions are gradually improving. But prosperity in full measure must await the satisfactory adjustment of accounts between debtor and creditor nations of the world and the restoration of international monetary standards, from which the acute financial difficulties have compelled a temporary departure.
Now I quote from the prorogation speech, session of 1932:
My government's policy of unemployment and farm relief, consistently and vigorously pur-
[Mr. Pouliot. 1
sued, has already achieved an amelioration of conditions and forecasts steady and continued improvement in both agrarian and industrial communities.
The larger the number of unemployed the rosier became the speeches from the throne. Now I come to the speech from the throne at the opening of the session of 1932-33:
The problem of unemployment continues to receive the anxious attention of my ministers. Under the powers granted them at the last session of parliament, they have been able to develop further, in cooperation with the provinces and municipalities, a scheme of direct relief to be put into operation during the autumn and winter months to the extent required by prevailing conditions. Plans for the re-establishment of the unemployed in various parts of the country are in preparation and will become operative as soon as, in the opinion of my ministers, the public expenditure incident thereto will be productive of commensurate benefits.
In January of 1932 the number of individuals on relief was 714,000; in January of 1933, that number had increased to 1,306,000. That was great progress I During the session of 1932-33 the Ottawa trade agreements were enacted, and the prorogation speech that year contained these words:
The courage with which the Canadian people have endured the burdens imposed upon them in these troubled times is witness to their great faith in the future of this country.
They should have faith, indeed.
It is, however, realized that cooperation amongst the peoples of the world is essential to recovery from the unprecedented conditions which have for so long prevailed in all countries.
Now I quote from the speech from the throne at the opening of the session in 1934:
The representatives of the various provinces strongly approve of the arrangements made by my government to care for single, unemployed, homeless men in camps until such time as they could be absorbed in industry, by providing them with employment on undertakings for the national good; and of the provision made in 1932 for settlement of families on the land, which has been extended with satisfactory results. My government propose further to promote employment by expenditures on essential public works and undertakings throughout the dominion.
Did that mean that the previous works imposed by the leader of the Tory party on the provinces and municipalities, and carried on by the joint expenditure of federal, provincial and municipal governments, were unessential and even useless? But this is no time to look backward, says the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett).
The speech continues:
I congratulate you that such improved world conditions are reflected in Canada by expanding trade, improving revenues, increasing employment, and a more confident outlook upon the

The Budget-Mr. Pouliot
future. Canada occupies a leading position amongst those countries where the evidence of a return to permanent prosperity is most convincing.
Then, from the prorogation speech in 1934:
The progressive improvement of general economic conditions in Canada which is presently much in evidence gives every indication of continuing in increasing measure.
Then, from the opening speech from the throne in 1935, the last year in which the previous government held office:
During the past year the grip of hard times has been broken. Conditions show marked improvement. Employment is increasing. Our trade is expanding. The national revenues are higher. These evidences of recovery attest the wisdom and efficacy of the measures you have taken. In these improved conditions, there may now successfully be carried forward those great tasks of reform upon which the well-being of this country depends.
And from the prorogation speech of that year:
The enactment of the measure relating to unemployment and social insurance will, through the establishment of a national labour exchange service, provide for dealing more effectively with the problem of seasonal and other unemployment, and will afford the means whereby Canadian workers can, with the assistance of the government, make provision for their own security.
That was the proposal, and the answer of the Canadian people to it was No, even before the Privy Council declared the measure was useless.
We must remember, sir, that in 1930 the leader of the Tory party stated there were
117,000	so-called unemployed. In March, 1935, the number on relief-and we have no figures about the unemployed part-time workers and the unemployed who were not on relief-was 1,258,421. Great progress! Twice a year, in the opening speech from the throne and in the prorogation speech, we were told that business was getting better and better, and yet the number of unemployed was increasing all the time.
To be fair let us compare the record of the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) with the record of the government which held office before him. He said that when he assumed office he would end unemployment. When he took office the total number of unemployed, including unemployables, stood at 117,000; when he left office it stood at about 1,300,000.

Now let us come to the municipalities. They have considered the question of unemployment from what angle? From the angle of finance. I am. in favour of investigating commissions, but managing commissions are sometimes dangerous. We have an employment commission. Let me tell the house that I do not believe much in that commission. It is a window-dressing commission, with the home improvement plan-and walking down Sparks street the other day I was much surprised to see a sign on which were the words "admission free" stuck in a bath room. That seemed strange, because few people appreciate such window dressing invitations when there are other windows showing fireplaces where the sign would be much more appropriate.
The question has been asked about the number of unemployed. On February 8 of this year I asked this question:
1.	What is actually the total number: (a) of heads of families; (b) of their dependents; (e) of individual cases of unemployed, all receiving relief at the present time?
2.	How many of the three above mentioned classes are employable?

Mr. Rogers:	All available information was
included in the report of the National Employment Commission with respect to the registration of recipients of direct relief which was tabled in the house on the 5th day of February. As other data is abstracted from the registration returns it w-ill be made available.
I thank the minister for the copy of the return, but I must say it contains no information about the previous occupations of the unemployed. Therefore it is of no use at all. I cannot see its usefulness as it does not 6how what the unemployed can do, or how they

can be employed. This is a very important point and one that should not be overlooked.

Mr. Young would be able to render much better service to the state on the tariff board, and he would be exceedingly well qualified for such a position. Mr. Tom Moore received only $228.95 for travelling expenses, no living allowance being paid. What a great sacrifice he made to serve the state. Apparently he served without salary. But he received $9,000 for doing nothing on the social insurance commission. He received nearly as much in salary as the four commissioners received in living allowances. They received a total of $9,728 while Mr. Moore received $9,000. I saw in the Ottawa citizen not long ago that he was no longer a member of the employment insurance commission, due to the ruling of the privy council, but was to be employed at a salary of $7,300 per year. He was to get $20 a day for 365 days. Apparently he is to work on Sundays. Our Lord created the universe in six days, but on the seventh He took a rest. Tom Moore is doing nothing for 365 days; therefore he does not need a weekly rest.
The creation of the employment commission was just as laudable an effort on the part of this government as were silly the increases made in the tariff by the previous government and its so-called social legislation which was knocked out recently by the privy council.
The speech of the Minister of Labour on the second reading of the employment commission bill on March 30 last year shows that he is fully qualified for his position. I would be quite willing to give him blanket authority to study this whole matter and report to the house. He is a reliable Minister of Labour and I am very sorry that in order to relieve unemployment all he has by way of assistance is a commission which is really more of an obstacle than a help.
Enough has been said already with regard to the abstract side of unemployment. I intend to refer to the individuals concerned. I have received a number of letters from unemployed people, which I should like to read if I had the time to do so. In his speech in support of his amendment, the

The Budget-Mr. Pouliot
leader of the Tory party, otherwise known as the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Bennett), made one suggestion. Was it constructive or was it not? Let us see. He said that the bureau of statistics was the place one would expect to go to for the purpose of getting information regarding the numbers of the unemployed. The last information gathered by the bureau of statistics in this connection was during the census of 1931. Therefore, the only information the bureau can supply in this regard would be that relating to 1931. The leader of the opposition did not even dare to quote that information when speaking on the unemployment and social insurance bill. If he does not know where to get the necessary information, it is not surprising that he never got it. After having been Prime Minister for five years he seems to know very little about this matter.
The proper source of this information is the municipalities. This government has authority to collect the necessary information from that source. All the government needs to do is to tell the provinces that they will get no more subsidies unless they provide the necessary information.
I should like to tell the house what in my humble opinion should be done. There should be a classification of the unemployed in each part of the country according to trades. We should have the number of unemployed in the building trades, unemployed factory workers, labourers, merchants, office help, professional workers, railway workers, technicians, iron and steel workers, longshoremen, miners, seamen, fishermen, domestics and sundry other occupations. It is very important to know the previous occupations of the unemployed! in order to know what can be done for them!.
I would suggest that this question of unemployment should be studied by a committee of this house. After having looked over the record I am surprised to find that during the last few years this question has not been considered by a committee of members of this house. I have before me a list of the different matters referred to the committee on industrial and international relations. In 1928 there was referred to it the question of insurance against unemployment and sickness, and the civil service councils, Bill No. 4; in 1929, grants of family allowances, and insurance against unemployment, sickness and invalidity; in 1930, Bill No. 39, respecting government contracts; in 1931, there was referred to it the resolution by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Miss Macphail) regarding promotion of peace by instituting professorships and 31111-toij
scholarships in Canadian universities. In 1932 it had no sittings; in 1933, no sittings; in 1934, no sittings. In 1935 there was referred to it the resolution on oriental seamen on Canadian ships, and the resolution for pensions for the blind. In 1936 there was referred to it a report of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and. the matter of employment of Canadian citizens on subsidized Canadian ships. In 1937 there have been no sittings as yet.
I should like to give particulars of the special committees of this house which have been set up to study various matters. In 1929 committees were set up to study the Dominion Elections Act, 1920, and the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act. In 1930 committees were set up to study the Dominion Elections Act. 1920; pensions and returned soldiers' problems. The special committees set up in 1931 studied the Beauharnois power project, and Bill No. 4, the Copyright Act In 1932 special consideration was given to the Bankruptcy Act, Bill No. 41; the civil service and Civil Service Act; certain charges and allegations made by Hon. G. N. Gordon; radio broadcasting; unfair competition in trade and commerce;' and Bill No. 4, to amend the Patent Act. During the session of 1932-33 special committees considered Bill No. 78 concerning pensions, and Bill No. 2 to amend the Representation Act. In 1934, special consideration was given to the Civil Service Act; price spreads and mass buying; operation of the radio act, elections and franchise acts. In 1935, consideration was given to the British North America Act; Bill No. 98 concerning the grain board; and housing. In 1936, we had under consideration the election and franchise acts, 1934; pensions and returned soldiers' problems; the marketing of wheat and other grains; and the radio commission.
In 1937, there are committees considering the elections and franchise acts; criminal code (death penalty) bill; farm implements.
It is an omission on the part of all of us, every hon. member is blameworthy, because a reference on the unemployment problem can be submitted to a committee on the motion of any hon. member, seconded by another, and adopted. This session is nearly over, but I hope that next session a motion will be carried for a committee to study unemployment at large. I humbly proffer this suggestion. The membership jf this house comes from every part of the country and represents every walk of life, and it seems to me that we could give a hand and substantial help to the government by studying this whole matter ourselves, rather than by referring it to others.
The Budget-Mr. Pouliot

We could formulate our suggestions without reference to party politics, as an assembly of members desiring to consider and come to definite conclusions on this vital problem in order to assist the government of the day.
Here was a suggestion that was made on April 30 to assist the government. A member of this house has done part of the work which is to be assigned to the National Employment Commisison. He is still ready to do that work for nothing-the classification of the unemployed according to their trades-if the government is willing, provided that he can pick up a staff to assist him in his work. It will save the government of the country $125,000. The offer is still good.

I cannot name him
because I fear to hurt his modesty.
We should also make an inventory of our natural resources, an investigation of packing, et cetera.
The trade policy of the government is excellent; and I am sure that if a committee of this house decided to study the whole matter from a non-partisan point of view, examining facts instead of theories, it would achieve very satisfactory results.
May I say in conclusion that as the trade policy of the government is very good there is no reason why its unemployment policy should not be of equal merit. In order to arrive at such a policy, however, we should get rid of any managing commission, and appoint an investigating committee from among ourselves to report back to the house in due course.
